lessons.plain: Before a team builds anything, someone has to be sure the right problem is being solved. A business problem is a gap between how things work now and how the organization needs them to work, and it causes real harm. An opportunity is a chance to gain something the organization does not yet have. This objective is about describing that problem or chance clearly, checking the description with the people involved, and then drawing a line around what the solution will and will not cover. That written line is the solution scope statement, the agreement everyone reads the same way before work starts.
lessons.guessPrompt: A sponsor says: 'Our customer support team is slow, so we need a new ticketing tool.' Before any teaching, what is one question you would ask before agreeing to buy a tool, and why?
lessons.teach:
A business problem is a gap that hurts the organization, described by its symptoms and effects rather than by a fix. An opportunity is a possible gain, described by what it would be worth. A root cause is the underlying reason the symptom happens. Five whys is a technique where you ask why repeatedly, each answer becoming the next question, until you reach a cause someone can act on. A problem statement is a short written description that names the problem, who it affects, its impact, and what a good outcome looks like, without naming a product. A solution scope statement lists what the solution will deliver, what is out of scope, and the key assumptions and constraints.

The approach works because a fix chosen before the cause is known often treats a symptom and leaves the real problem in place. Worked example: average support ticket wait is three days. Why? Agents spend time searching for old notes. Why? Notes live in three places. Why? No shared knowledge base was ever set up. The root cause is scattered storage, not tool speed. Problem statement: scattered support notes affect agents and customers, causing three-day waits and lower satisfaction scores. Scope: in, consolidating notes for the two support queues; out, billing system changes and phone routing.

A common mistake is writing the solution into the problem statement, such as 'we need a new tool.' This locks the scope before the cause is known. In a running system, the consequence is that a tool gets bought, the notes stay scattered, and out-of-scope items return later as change requests that the team must absorb or reject.

questions.prompt: A regional dental clinic sees about 40 missed appointments a week. The team asked why, and the answers were: patients are not reminded; reminder texts are sent by hand from a spreadsheet; the spreadsheet is refreshed only on Fridays; the scheduling system's export to that spreadsheet was never automated, so that is the root cause. The team has written this problem statement: manual reminder preparation affects clinic staff and patients, causing about 40 missed appointments a week. The team has also written one in-scope item: automating the weekly export for the two named clinics. The scope statement still needs its out-of-scope entries. Which item should be recorded as out of scope?
choices: Changes to the billing and insurance claims module
Refreshing the spreadsheet by hand each Friday until the export is live
Automating the weekly export for the two named clinics
The wording of the problem statement about 40 missed appointments
questions.why: Billing and claims processing is unrelated to the reminder chain, so it belongs in the out-of-scope list, while the other three are either in scope or are not scope items at all.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, how does a business opportunity differ from a business problem when a team writes a needs-assessment statement?
choices: An opportunity is described by the value it could gain, while a problem is described by its symptoms and effects
An opportunity is described by its symptoms, while a problem is described by the value it could gain
An opportunity is a cause someone can act on, while a problem is a list of who the change affects
Both are described by the solution the team plans to build, so the difference is only in the budget
questions.why: The teaching text defines a problem by its symptoms and effects and an opportunity by what it would be worth, so the first option reversed is wrong and the others mix up causes, solutions, or budgets.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's analyst writes the problem statement as: We need a new route-planning software product. Later, during review, the team finds that the real cause is outdated delivery zone maps. What is the most likely consequence for the running system?
choices: The problem statement becomes more accurate because it already names the product that fixes the cause
The scope is locked before the cause is known, so the product gets bought while the outdated maps remain and out-of-scope items come back as change requests
The root cause is solved automatically once the product is bought, so no scope review is needed
The team must remove the root cause from the five whys chain because only the product name matters
questions.why: Naming a solution in the problem statement locks the scope before the cause is known, so the tool may be bought while the real cause persists and out-of-scope items return later as change requests.

questions.prompt: A warehouse has late shipments. A team asks why repeatedly. Answers: orders are picked late; pickers wait for carts; only nine carts are assigned across two picking zones; the cart allocation was set when the warehouse had one zone. Which answer is the root cause the five whys technique should reach?
choices: Pickers are too slow at collecting items from the shelves
The warehouse needs a new picking app to track carts in real time
The cart allocation was set for one zone and never updated for two zones
Late shipments, because the outbound trucks leave at a fixed time
questions.why: The five whys technique stops at a cause someone can act on, and the outdated cart allocation is that cause, whereas the other options are symptoms or solutions chosen before the cause is known.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to the project how you would move from a vague request, such as 'we need a faster report,' to a solution scope statement. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking what the report is failing to do today and who is harmed, so the request becomes a problem with evidence rather than a demand for a feature. Then I would ask why that failure happens, repeating the question until I reach a cause the team can act on. Often the answer is about data, timing, or approvals, not speed. Once the problem is stated without naming a fix, I would write the scope statement: what the solution covers, what it explicitly leaves out, and which assumptions it depends on. The tradeoff is time. This analysis takes effort up front, and stakeholders who want quick delivery may see it as delay. I would accept that cost, but I would keep the review short and tie each question to a decision the sponsor has to make.
rubricPoints: Separates the stated request from the underlying business problem or opportunity
Uses a technique such as five whys to find a root cause rather than a symptom
Writes a problem statement that names impact and affected people without naming a solution
Defines both in-scope and out-of-scope items along with key assumptions
Names a real tradeoff, such as time spent up front versus delivery pressure

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers business problem analysis, and explaining a scope statement back to a teammate is the core skill.

lessons.plain: A value proposition is the short, honest answer to the question 'why should we build this, and what do we get back for the cost?' Before anyone designs a solution, a business analyst gathers facts from several places: the people who feel the problem, the records that show what is actually happening, and the costs and risks of doing nothing. Then they check those facts against each other and state the expected benefit in terms the sponsor can test later. Think of a home buyer who compares a house's price with what it would really give them to live in, rather than just liking the paint colour.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team wants a new scheduling tool because it would be nice to have. Name two different places you would look for evidence that the tool is worth its cost, and say why relying on only one of them would not be enough.
lessons.teach:
Definition. A value proposition for an initiative is a statement of the measurable benefit an organisation expects from a change, set against what that change costs and risks. Collecting and analysing information from varied sources means gathering evidence about that benefit from more than one kind of place, then testing the pieces against each other. The main sources are people (interviews, workshops, surveys of staff who do the work), documents and records (reports, ticket histories, financial figures), observed behaviour (watching how work is really done rather than how people say it is done), and external inputs (market data, regulatory requirements). A baseline is the measured starting point before any change, and it is what lets you prove a benefit later.

Why it works. No single source is reliable alone. Interviews capture opinion and can overstate pain. Records show what happened but not why. Observation reveals workarounds people no longer mention. When two or more independent sources point to the same gap, the claimed benefit becomes credible. Confirming a fact by viewing it from several independent angles is called triangulation.

Worked example. A regional dispatch team says the old routing screen costs them time. Step 1: an interview suggests each job setup feels slow. Step 2: a timesheet export shows average setup at 14 minutes against a 9-minute target. Step 3: observation shows dispatchers re-typing addresses into a second window. Step 4: the value proposition states that removing the re-typing step could recover about five minutes per job, measured against the 14-minute baseline, a figure the sponsor can check after go-live.

Common mistake. Treating the most vocal stakeholder's opinion as the value, and writing a benefit with no baseline, so nobody can later tell whether it was achieved.

Consequence. Without a baseline, the project cannot show a return after delivery, and funding for the next phase becomes hard to justify. A value proposition is only as strong as the evidence trail behind it.

questions.prompt: A city library is considering a self-checkout kiosk to reduce queues. Three pieces of evidence are already in hand. Staff in a survey say the desk is always busy. Circulation records show about 3,200 checkouts a week, with the heaviest load from 4 to 6 pm. Observation during those hours shows patrons waiting about 11 minutes at the desk on average. The business analyst has not yet written the value proposition. Which step completes it?
choices: Adopt the survey staff's estimate that the kiosk would save 20 minutes per patron, because staff know the desk best.
Skip any baseline and measure the wait once the kiosk is installed, then decide afterward whether the benefit was real.
Set the benefit as cutting the peak-hour wait from the measured 11 minutes by a stated amount, then weigh that gain against the kiosk's cost and risks.
Describe the benefit as better patron satisfaction, since a figure would be guesswork before the kiosk is installed.
questions.why: A value proposition sets a measurable benefit against a measured baseline and weighs it against cost and risk, which is what option C does using the 11-minute observed wait.

questions.prompt: In a value proposition, what is a baseline?
choices: The budget ceiling the sponsor has agreed to for the initiative.
The measured starting point before any change, which later shows whether a benefit was achieved.
The list of stakeholders who were interviewed during needs assessment.
The external market average that the organisation hopes to match.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a baseline as the measured starting point before any change, and says it is what lets you prove a benefit later.

questions.prompt: A department head tells the analyst that a new patient intake form will save every nurse 30 minutes a shift. No time records were pulled, no one watched the current process, and the claim rests only on the head's own impression. What is the main weakness?
choices: The form has not yet been approved by the regulator, which is the only thing that matters.
The claim rests on one source of opinion, with no baseline and no independent source to confirm it.
The claim is too modest, because a 30-minute saving is usually an underestimate for intake forms.
The analyst should have surveyed patients instead of nurses, since patients feel the delay.
questions.why: A single opinion without a baseline or a second independent source, such as records or observation, cannot be trusted as evidence of value, so option D names the real weakness.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm wants to justify a barcode scanner for its warehouse. Which set of evidence best supports a credible value proposition through triangulation?
choices: A vendor brochure claiming scanners cut picking errors, plus the warehouse manager's belief that errors are rare.
Mispick counts from the last year's records, observed picking sessions showing workers checking paper lists twice, and a staff survey on perceived error frequency.
A single week of timing data from the night shift only, with no records from other shifts.
Staff interviews about how tiring the job feels, plus a survey of the scanner's colour options.
questions.why: Triangulation means confirming a fact from several independent angles, and option C combines records, observation, and staff perception, while the other options rely on one source or on vendor claims.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who believes value is whatever the sponsor says it is: how you would collect and check the evidence behind an initiative's value proposition, and one limit of the approach you chose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not take the sponsor's view as the value on its own. I would collect evidence from at least three kinds of source: interviews with the people doing the work, records such as ticket histories or timesheets that give a measured baseline, and direct observation of how the task is actually performed, including workarounds. Where those sources agree on the same gap, I would write the benefit as a number tied to that baseline, so it can be checked after delivery. The limit is cost and time: triangulating takes effort, and a small sample of observation may miss rare situations. I would say so openly, state the assumptions, and flag which parts of the value are still weakly supported.
rubricPoints: Collects evidence from several different kinds of source rather than one
Uses triangulation to confirm a benefit across independent sources
Ties the stated benefit to a measured baseline so it can be verified later
Names a real limit, such as effort, sample size, or unvalidated assumptions

suggested.rationale: Explaining the evidence trail back to a teammate is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine practises business value analysis.

lessons.plain: Before anyone builds anything, the team needs to agree on what the work is for. This objective is about working with the people who own a project to write down its goals and objectives (the outcomes they want, stated so you can later tell whether they happened), pin down the business need behind them (the gap between how things are and how the organization needs them to be), and draw the boundary of the solution scope (what the product will and will not do). Think of it like agreeing on the destination, the reason for the trip, and which roads are included before anyone buys a map. When these line up with the organization's broader strategy, the product is far more likely to earn its keep.
lessons.guessPrompt: A sponsor says 'we need a faster customer portal.' Before you start gathering requirements, what two or three questions would you ask to turn that into a goal and a boundary the team can actually check?
lessons.teach:
A goal is a broad statement of the outcome an organization wants, such as keeping more customers. An objective is a measurable step toward that goal, such as reducing the average time to resolve a support ticket to under two days within six months. A business need is the underlying gap between the current state and the desired state that justifies the work. Solution scope is the set of capabilities the proposed product must deliver, together with an explicit list of what is out of scope. Business analysts collaborate with sponsors, users and other stakeholders to confirm these items, because each one constrains the rest.

Why this works: goals are hard to test, so objectives make them checkable, and an explicit scope boundary stops the product from quietly absorbing every request. When the need, goals and scope are written down and agreed, each later requirement can be traced back to a reason.

Worked example. A sponsor says the call-centre team wants fewer repeat calls. Step 1: name the goal, improve first-contact resolution. Step 2: name the objective, raise first-contact resolution from 60 to 75 percent within two quarters. Step 3: state the need, agents lack order history during calls, so customers repeat themselves. Step 4: draw the scope, the product shows order history and open tickets to agents, but does not change billing or refunds, which stay out of scope. Step 5: check alignment, since the company strategy is customer retention, the objective supports it.

Common mistake: writing the solution before the need, such as 'build a new CRM' with no stated gap. Then nobody can say whether the product succeeded.

Consequence in a running system: an unclear scope lets a team add a feature such as refund processing to a live service without the load, security and audit reviews it needs, so the release slips or breaks an unrelated process. The product should be judged against the need it was written to meet.

questions.prompt: A regional food bank wants volunteers to keep showing up for weekend shifts. Work through the steps. Step 1, the goal: keep volunteers coming back. Step 2, the objective: raise the shift confirmation rate from 70 to 85 percent within 90 days. Step 3, the need: reminder texts go out only the night before, so volunteers forget and leave shifts uncovered. Step 4, the scope: this is missing. Step 5, the alignment check: the food bank's strategy is reliable weekly distribution, so the objective supports it. Which choice correctly completes Step 4?
choices: Build a reminder service that sends texts at three set times, and state that donor tracking, van routing and payroll are out of scope.
Add every volunteer request from the last year to the build so nothing is missed.
Choose a texting vendor with the lowest monthly fee before writing any scope.
Restate the goal of keeping volunteers returning so the scope is clear.
questions.why: Step 4 names the capabilities the product must deliver and lists what is explicitly out of scope, which is the boundary the teaching text describes, while the other choices either absorb every request, skip scope, or repeat the goal.

questions.prompt: A sponsor at a small logistics firm says the team should make the warehouse run better. Which statement is an objective, meaning a measurable step toward a goal?
choices: Improve the overall operations of the site.
Cut the pick-error rate from 2 percent to under 1 percent within six months.
Replace the handheld scanners with a new tablet system.
Make the warehouse run better.
questions.why: An objective must be measurable and time-bound, so only the statement with a specific current value, target and deadline qualifies; the others are goals or solutions.

questions.prompt: A team has started building a feature to export data to payroll. The agreed scope list does not mention payroll, and a stakeholder now asks for it mid-build, saying it will only take a day. What should the business analyst do first?
choices: Add the feature, since a one-day change cannot affect the rest of the work.
Check the agreed scope and raise the request as a scope decision with the sponsor before any build work.
Ignore the request because scope is fixed once development starts.
Build it quietly and measure whether anyone uses it before deciding.
questions.why: An explicit scope boundary exists so that additions are judged against it, meaning the analyst should compare the request to the agreed scope and escalate it as a decision rather than absorb it silently or ignore it.

questions.prompt: A company's strategy is to lower its cost per delivered order. Which proposed objective best supports that strategy?
choices: Launch a premium branded packaging line by the end of the year.
Hire ten more customer service staff to answer general enquiries.
Increase the number of social media followers by 40 percent within a year.
Reduce the average number of failed delivery attempts from 12 percent to 6 percent within two quarters.
questions.why: Fewer failed delivery attempts directly lowers the cost per delivered order, so it is a measurable objective that serves the stated strategy, while the others either do not affect cost or raise it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a business need, a measurable objective and a solution scope differ, and name one tradeoff a team faces when it draws the scope boundary too tightly or too loosely.
lessons.modelAnswer: A business need is the gap between where the organization is and where it needs to be, such as agents repeating questions because they cannot see order history. The objective is the measurable target that shows the gap is closing, such as first-contact resolution rising from 60 to 75 percent. The solution scope is what the product will deliver to get there, with an explicit out-of-scope list. The tradeoff lies in how tight the boundary is. Drawn too tightly, the product may miss the need and users will build workarounds. Drawn too loosely, scope creep adds work and delays the release. Good practice is to tie every in-scope item back to a stated need and revisit the boundary with the sponsor when new requests arrive.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes a business need, a goal or objective, and a solution scope
Notes that an objective must be measurable so progress can be checked
Explains that scope includes an explicit out-of-scope boundary
Names a tradeoff of tight versus loose scope and links in-scope items to the stated need

suggested.rationale: Explaining the need, objective and scope in your own words to a teammate is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine practises it.

lessons.plain: A stakeholder is anyone who can affect a project or be affected by it: the person paying for it, the people who will use it, the staff who will run it, and the regulators who can block it. Identifying stakeholders means going through the project's written goals, its measurable objectives, and its requirements, and asking for each one who cares about it, who wants it to succeed, and who would notice if it failed. The aim is to make sure the right people are involved in decisions and kept informed, so nobody important learns late that their needs were ignored. Think of it like checking the guest list before an event: you look at what the event is for, then ask who it touches.
lessons.guessPrompt: A dental clinic wants a new online booking system with the goal 'patients can book and change appointments without phoning the front desk.' Before reading on, name three groups of people you would want to hear from about this project, and say why each one matters.
lessons.teach:
A stakeholder is any person or group with an interest in an initiative, who can influence it, or who is affected by it. A goal is a broad, lasting business aim. An objective is a specific, measurable target that supports a goal. A requirement is a stated need or condition the solution must meet. Each of these three items points to people. Someone wants the goal met, someone owns the objective's measurement, and someone must live with the requirement. Tracing from these statements to people finds parties you would miss if you only thought of 'the users.'

Worked example. Goal: reduce phone traffic at the front desk. Objective: 60 percent of bookings made online within six months. Requirement: patients can reschedule with 24 hours notice. Step one: the goal points to front desk staff, who are affected and want fewer calls. Step two: the objective points to the clinic manager, who owns and measures the target. Step three: the requirement points to dentists, whose calendars must reflect changes, and to patients, who use the system. Step four: the requirement implies an integration, so the records and IT team is a stakeholder. Step five: because patient health data is involved, the privacy officer is a stakeholder.

Common mistake: listing only the people who are easy to reach or the loudest in meetings, and forgetting those who are indirectly affected or who may lose out, such as auditors, insurers, or staff whose tasks disappear. Consequence: a missed stakeholder usually surfaces after build, when the privacy officer finds the form breaks data rules, forcing costly rework.

A complete stakeholder list is the foundation for deciding whose needs get weighed and who must be told about changes.

questions.prompt: A regional bus operator is replacing paper ticket sales with a phone app. Goal: keep fare revenue steady while cutting cash handling. Objective: 70 percent of fares paid through the app within nine months, measured by the finance team's monthly report. Requirement: drivers can validate a ticket even when there is no mobile signal. Step one: the goal points to the finance director, who wants revenue steady. Step two: the objective points to the head of fare operations, who owns the measurement. Step three: the offline requirement points to drivers, who must validate tickets on the bus. Step four is missing from this trace and is the one you must identify. Which choice is that missing step?
choices: The bus manufacturer, because older buses may not support the app.
The passengers, who were already named as users in the goal, so no new party is added.
The marketing team, because they will advertise the new app to riders.
The mobile device team, because the offline requirement means fare data must be stored on the validator and kept current, which that team builds and supports.
questions.why: An offline requirement implies local data storage on the device, and the team that builds and supports that device and its data store is a stakeholder the requirement points to, while the other choices either do not follow from the requirement or repeat a party already named.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines a stakeholder in an initiative?
choices: Only the person who signs off the budget for the initiative.
Only the people who will use the finished solution day to day.
Any outside vendor that supplies software or hardware to the initiative.
Any person or group with an interest in the initiative, who can influence it, or who is affected by it.
questions.why: A stakeholder is defined by interest, influence, or being affected, which is broader than budget authority, end users only, or vendors.

questions.prompt: A city utility is adding a web form so customers can dispute a water bill online within 14 days. A reviewer is checking which parties the requirement points to. Which of these is the best example of a party the requirement points to?
choices: The newsletter editor, who publishes monthly resident updates.
The customer service agents who currently take bill disputes by phone and will see those calls move to the web form.
The city council member who announced the program in a press release.
The city's landscaping contractor, who maintains the parks.
questions.why: The requirement changes how disputes are handled, so the agents whose work shifts to the new form are directly affected, while the other options have no link to the bill dispute requirement.

questions.prompt: A school district is launching an attendance app that teachers and parents will use. The initial review named only teachers and parents, and the app must send attendance records into the existing student information system. Which party is the most important addition to the review?
choices: The administrator who owns the student records system and its data rules.
The company that runs the school bus routes.
The coach who organises after-school sports.
The local newspaper's education reporter.
questions.why: The integration requirement means the owner of the student records system is affected and holds the data rules, so missing this party is the classic gap that surfaces late as rework.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would move from a project's goals, objectives and requirements to a list of stakeholders, and name one limit or tradeoff of that approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the goal, then read each objective and requirement and ask who wants it met, who owns its measurement, who must act on it, and who is affected if it changes. Each answer becomes a stakeholder entry, and I also note whether that person needs to be actively involved or only kept informed. I then check for gaps by looking at groups that touch the system indirectly, such as compliance, support, and finance. The main limit is that the list is only as good as the written goals and requirements. If those are vague or incomplete, I will miss stakeholders whose interest is implied rather than stated. So I treat the first list as a draft and confirm it with the sponsor and a few people from each group before relying on it.
rubricPoints: Traces each goal, objective, or requirement to the people who want it met, own it, or are affected by it.
Distinguishes stakeholders who need active involvement from those who only need to be informed.
Checks for indirectly affected parties such as compliance, support, or finance.
Names a real limit, such as dependence on the quality of the written goals and requirements, and how to mitigate it.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a realistic scenario about who a change touches adds the most here, and no current OpsForge mission or planned engine covers stakeholder identification.

lessons.plain: When a project is about to change how people work, each person affected wants something from it and would lose something if it went badly. Stakeholder values are those wants, described in terms of what each person gains. Eliciting them means drawing them out through conversations, workshops, surveys, document review, or watching people do their work, rather than guessing. The result is a starting record of who cares about what and how much, so later decisions about which requirements to build first have a fair reference point. Think of it as a snapshot of everyone's priorities taken before anyone starts arguing for their favourite feature.
lessons.guessPrompt: A hospital's scheduling project has three requests: nurses want fewer clicks per booking, the finance office wants fewer missed appointments that go unbilled, and patients want shorter waits on the phone. Which request would you rank first, and what would you need to know before deciding?
lessons.teach: A stakeholder is any person or group who can affect an initiative or is affected by it, such as end users, sponsors, operations staff, auditors, or regulators. A value is the benefit a stakeholder expects to receive, stated in their own terms: time saved, risk avoided, money earned, or a rule followed. Elicitation is the set of techniques used to draw this information out of people and documents, including interviews, facilitated workshops, surveys, document review, and observing work as it happens. A baseline here means a recorded starting point: a list of stakeholders, the values each one holds, and a rough relative weight for each value. It is the reference against which requirements are later ranked. Why this works: people often state a solution, such as add a button, rather than the value behind it, such as fewer missed calls. Asking why each request matters turns a wish into a value that can be compared with others. When values from different stakeholders are recorded in the same terms, conflicts become visible early and can be resolved before build work starts. Worked example: a clinic wants a new appointment-booking system. Step one, identify stakeholders: patients, front-desk staff, nurses, and the billing office. Step two, elicit: interview a front-desk clerk, who asks for fewer phone calls; ask why, and she says double-bookings cost the clinic money and staff time. Step three, record: the value is fewer double-bookings, with a high weight because it affects revenue and workload. Step four, repeat for billing and patients, then compare. Requirements that serve several high-weight values rise to the top. Common mistake: recording the loudest or most senior voice as the baseline, or stopping at the requested feature. Consequence: requirements get ranked against a skewed baseline, so the team builds what was argued for rather than what delivers the most value, and the same dispute returns at every review. A baseline built from elicited values, rather than from the loudest voice, is what makes later prioritization defensible.

questions.prompt: A regional food bank is replacing its donor-tracking spreadsheet. Three stakeholder groups were identified: the warehouse lead, the volunteer coordinator, and the grants office. The warehouse lead asked for a barcode scanner. Asked why, she said weekly stock counts are off by about 15 cases, so the team cannot tell what to hand out. Her value is recorded as 'accurate weekly stock counts', weight high. The volunteer coordinator's value, recorded in the same terms, is 'shift sign-ups confirmed 48 hours ahead', weight medium. The grants office's value is 'quarterly spending reports that match the ledger', weight high. One step is still missing before requirements can be ranked. Which step is it?
choices: Rewrite the grants office value as a feature request so it can be built.
Count how many stakeholders mentioned a barcode scanner to set its weight.
Ask the executive director which value matters most and drop the others from the baseline.
Compare the recorded values against each other to find conflicts that must be resolved before build starts.
questions.why: The baseline is only useful once values from different stakeholders are compared in the same terms, because that comparison is what exposes conflicts early.

questions.prompt: In the sense used for prioritizing requirements, what is a baseline?
choices: The final set of test results that shows which requirements passed.
A signed budget that caps how many requirements a project may include.
A list of approved requirements arranged in the order they will be built.
A recorded starting point listing stakeholders, the values each holds, and a rough relative weight for each value.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a baseline as a recorded starting point of stakeholders, their values, and relative weights, used as the reference for ranking requirements later.

questions.prompt: A product owner for a municipal parking-permit app skips interviews and uses the feature list from the deputy director's email as the baseline. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: Requirements are ranked by who argued loudest, so the baseline is skewed and the same dispute returns at each review.
Stakeholder values are reconciled automatically once the deputy director signs off on the list.
The app ships faster and delivers the same total value, because fewer people were consulted.
Elicitation is no longer needed, because the email already names who is affected.
questions.why: Recording the loudest or most senior voice as the baseline skews later ranking, so the team builds what was argued for and the dispute recurs, as the teaching text warns.

questions.prompt: A transit agency stakeholder asks for a red-amber-green status panel on a fleet dashboard. Asked why, they say they need to spot buses running late for maintenance before they fail on the road. Which entry is the value that belongs in the baseline?
choices: Breakdowns avoided by spotting maintenance-late buses early.
A red-amber-green status panel on the fleet dashboard.
The operations director's preference for visual reports.
Users want the dashboard built this quarter.
questions.why: The value is the benefit the stakeholder expects, stated in their terms, which here is avoiding breakdowns; the panel is only the solution they proposed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would determine stakeholder values for a new initiative and why that baseline matters for prioritizing requirements. Name one limit or tradeoff of the elicitation approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would first list every group affected by the initiative, including people who would not use the system directly, such as auditors or the support desk. For each group I would elicit values in a way that fits them: interviews for senior sponsors, observation for frontline staff, and a short survey where the group is large. For each stated request I would ask why it matters, so the record holds the benefit rather than the feature. I would then write each value in comparable terms and give it a rough relative weight, which becomes our baseline. That baseline is what lets us rank requirements against shared reference points instead of against whoever argued hardest. The tradeoff is time: thorough interviews across many groups take weeks, and surveys are faster but lose the reasons behind answers, so I would use surveys for breadth and interviews for the high-weight groups.
rubricPoints: Identifies stakeholders broadly, including indirect ones, before eliciting values
Converts stated requests into underlying values by asking why they matter
Records values in comparable terms with relative weights forming a baseline
Explains that the baseline anchors requirement prioritization and reduces dispute
Names a real limit or tradeoff of the chosen elicitation method

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers stakeholder value analysis, so a worked exam-style scenario is the best available practice for this objective.

lessons.plain: Before a business analyst asks anyone what they want built, they first check why the work is being done at all. A business case is the written argument that a project is worth the money and effort, usually stating the problem, the expected benefit, and the options considered. Project goals are the specific outcomes the sponsors want reached. Reviewing both gives you context: who the work is for, what success looks like, and what is out of bounds. Without that context, requirements work drifts toward whatever the loudest person asks for.
lessons.guessPrompt: A sponsor hands you a request for a new inventory screen, but the business case you have not yet read is about reducing late deliveries. What would you check first, and why?
lessons.teach:
A business case is the document, or set of documents, that justifies a project: the problem or opportunity, the expected benefits, the options considered, and the cost and risk of each. Project goals are the measurable outcomes the project is meant to achieve, drawn from that case. Reviewing both means reading them before elicitation begins, so you know the purpose the requirements must serve. Elicitation means drawing out what stakeholders need, and it goes better when you already know the frame. Why it works: every requirement should trace back to a goal, and every goal back to a business need. Starting from the case lets you tell whether a requested feature moves a goal or merely looks useful.

Worked example: a regional delivery company's business case says late deliveries rose from 4 percent to 11 percent last year, and the goal is to bring late deliveries under 5 percent within twelve months. Step 1: note the problem (late deliveries) and the measure (percentage late). Step 2: note the scope boundary the case sets, which is dispatch and route planning only, not billing. Step 3: list the stakeholders the case names as affected, such as dispatchers, drivers and customer service. Step 4: when a warehouse manager asks for a new inventory screen, check it against the goal. It does not reduce late deliveries and sits outside scope, so it goes to a parking lot rather than becoming a requirement.

Common mistake: treating the business case as a finished document to file away, or treating the goals as the requirements themselves. The case explains why, the goals say what success looks like, and requirements say what the solution must do. Skipping the review means the analyst discovers the purpose late, after stakeholders have already agreed to unrelated features.

Consequence in a running system: if the context is missed, the team builds a dispatch feature that nobody measures against the late-delivery goal. When the late rate does not fall, no one can tell which requirements were responsible.

The business case is the reference point that the rest of the business analysis work must answer to.

questions.prompt: A university library's business case says no-show rates for bookable study rooms rose from 6 percent to 14 percent in one year. The goal is to bring no-shows under 7 percent within six months. Step 1: the problem is missed room bookings, and the measure is the percentage of bookings not used. Step 2: the case limits scope to room booking and reminder messages only, and excludes the catalogue and fines. Step 3: the case names students and front-desk staff as the affected groups. Step 4 is missing and must be done next: a catalogue team asks for a new search filter for journal articles, and the analyst has to decide what to do with it. Which completion is correct?
choices: Add it to the goals list, because it is measurable and the library wants it.
Delay the decision until the catalogue team has finished a full cost estimate, because scope is only fixed after budgeting.
Send it to the parking lot, because it neither reduces no-shows nor falls inside the booking scope the case sets.
Accept it as a requirement, because any feature that improves the student experience supports the business case.
questions.why: A request is checked against the goal and the scope boundary; a search filter does not move the no-show measure and sits outside booking scope, so it is parked rather than made a requirement.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's business case is filed by the sponsor and never opened again, while the analyst starts interviewing warehouse staff. What is the main risk of this approach?
choices: The interviews will take longer than planned, but the requirements will still be correct.
The analyst will not know the purpose the requirements must serve, so requests cannot be judged against it.
Stakeholders will refuse to be interviewed without a signed copy of the case.
The project sponsor will be required to rewrite the case in the analyst's format.
questions.why: Without reading the case and goals first, the analyst has no frame for telling which elicited needs serve the purpose, which is the point of reviewing it before elicitation.

questions.prompt: A hospital pharmacy's goal is to cut dispensing errors by 30 percent within a year. A nurse manager asks for a mobile app for ward staff to message pharmacists. What is the correct first move for the analyst?
choices: Ask whether the messaging app would move the error-reduction goal and sits within the scope set by the case, before accepting it as a requirement.
Convert the request into a new goal so it can be measured separately.
Build the app requirement immediately, since messaging is a stakeholder need.
Reject the request without discussion, since mobile apps are never in scope for pharmacy projects.
questions.why: The correct move is to test the request against the goal and the case's scope before treating it as a requirement, which is how the analyst tells useful features from merely attractive ones.

questions.prompt: A city parks department skipped reviewing its business case. Three months into elicitation, the team has signed off many features, but none of them is linked to the case's goal of raising park usage by 15 percent. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The goal will be revised automatically once enough features are signed off.
The features will be cheaper to build because they are unlinked to targets.
The case will be legally invalidated and the project must stop.
The team will be unable to tell which requirements, if any, are responsible when usage does not rise.
questions.why: Requirements not traced to a goal cannot be evaluated against it, so when the target is missed nobody can identify which requirements were responsible.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a new teammate why you review the business case and project goals before eliciting requirements, and name one limit or tradeoff of doing that review first.
lessons.modelAnswer: I review the business case and goals first because they tell me why the work exists and what success looks like, so every question I ask stays tied to that purpose. The tradeoff is time: a thorough review before elicitation delays the first stakeholder meetings, and a case written months ago may no longer match what the business wants. So I treat the case as the starting context, not the final word. I check the stated goals with the sponsor, confirm the scope boundaries, and note which stakeholders the case names. When a new request arrives, I can ask whether it moves a goal. If the case looks out of date, I flag it early rather than silently building against it. The review does not replace elicitation; it sets the frame that elicitation has to answer to.
rubricPoints: Business case explains why the project exists, including the problem, expected benefits and options considered.
Project goals are measurable outcomes drawn from the case and define what success looks like.
The review sets scope boundaries and identifies affected stakeholders before elicitation begins.
Each requirement is checked against goals so that it traces back to a business need.
Names a limit: the case may be outdated or incomplete and should be validated with sponsors.

suggested.rationale: Explaining why context comes before elicitation, and where that review falls short, is the core skill here and no listed mission or engine covers it directly.

lessons.plain: Requirements traceability means keeping a visible chain between each requirement and the things connected to it: the business need that caused it, the design or test that proves it, and any change requests that altered it. A traceability strategy is the agreed plan for how that chain is built and kept current on a project. It decides which links matter, how they are recorded, who maintains them, what tool holds them, and how often they are reviewed. Think of it as a family tree for requirements. When someone asks why a feature exists or what breaks if it changes, the tree answers without anyone digging through old meeting notes. The strategy also decides how much tree is worth building before the work starts.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has 140 requirements, and a stakeholder asks: If we drop requirement 37, what else breaks? Without any special tools, how would you find the answer, and what one setup choice would make that answer faster next time?
lessons.teach:
A trace link is a recorded connection between two items, such as a requirement and the business objective it serves. Upstream means toward the source of need, and downstream means toward the things built or checked because of the requirement. A traceability matrix is a grid or table that shows these links, often in a spreadsheet or in a requirements management tool. Attributes are the descriptive fields stored with each item, such as owner, status, priority, or release. Granularity is how fine-grained the items are. A traceability strategy sets these choices in advance so that the links are consistent.

Why it works: once each requirement points to its causes and its consequences, impact questions become lookups rather than investigations.

Worked example. Requirement REQ-037 says the dispatcher sees vehicle positions refreshed within 10 seconds. Step 1: trace upstream from REQ-037 to business objective BO-4, reduce missed pickups. Step 2: trace downstream to design element DE-12, the position refresh path. Step 3: trace downstream to test case TC-112, which checks the 10 second limit. Step 4: note that TC-112 is scheduled for release 2.1. When the stakeholder asks about dropping REQ-037, the list of DE-12, TC-112, and release 2.1 scope answers the question in minutes.

Common mistake: tracing everything at maximum detail, which makes the matrix too large to maintain, or building the links once at the start and never updating them after approved changes.

Consequence: if an approved change is not reflected in the links, a test may keep checking a dropped requirement while a new feature has no test, and the release can pass review with a coverage gap nobody can see.

A sound strategy names the link types to keep, the granularity, the tool, the owner of each link, and the review point.

questions.prompt: A regional credit union is building a loan-application system. Requirement REQ-210 says income documents are checked against the bank's rules before a loan officer opens the file. The team traces it as follows. Step 1: trace upstream from REQ-210 to business objective BO-7, shorten loan decision time. Step 2: trace downstream to design element DE-31, the document-check rule engine. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: note that TC-205 is scheduled for release 3.0, so the release 3.0 scope answers any question about dropping REQ-210. Which step fills the gap?
choices: Trace upstream from DE-31 back to BO-7 a second time to confirm the objective.
Delete DE-31 from the matrix so that the list stays short.
Record the owner and priority attributes of REQ-210 in the matrix.
Trace downstream from DE-31 to test case TC-205, which checks the document-check rule.
questions.why: Step 3 must follow the downstream chain from the design element to the test that checks it, which is the link the release scope depends on.

questions.prompt: A hospital's supply-ordering project has a requirement that links to a cost-saving objective. In traceability terms, which direction does that link run?
choices: Attribute, meaning a descriptive field stored with the requirement.
Granularity, meaning how fine-grained the requirement is.
Downstream, toward the things built from the requirement.
Upstream, toward the source of need that the requirement serves.
questions.why: Upstream means toward the source of need, and a link from a requirement to the objective it serves runs upstream.

questions.prompt: A transport company's team built its trace links at the start of a fleet-tracking project and never updated them after the steering committee approved a change that dropped a requirement. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: A test may keep checking the dropped requirement while a new feature has no test, and the coverage gap stays hidden.
The matrix becomes too large to maintain, so the team must stop tracing entirely.
The change is automatically reflected in every link, so no gap can occur.
The objective the requirement served is removed from the business case by default.
questions.why: Stale links after an approved change can leave a dropped requirement tested and a new feature untested, and the gap is invisible in the matrix.

questions.prompt: A school district is planning a bus-scheduling project. Which set of choices must a sound traceability strategy name in advance so that links stay consistent?
choices: Only the attributes stored with each item, such as owner and status.
The link types to keep, the granularity, the tool, the owner of each link, and the review point.
Every link at the finest possible detail, all kept in one spreadsheet.
The vendor contract terms, the project budget, and the number of stakeholders.
questions.why: The teaching text lists these five elements as what a sound strategy names, and setting them in advance keeps the links consistent.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is about to start requirements work what a traceability strategy should decide before any requirement is written, and name one limit or tradeoff of tracing too much.
lessons.modelAnswer: Before writing requirements, I would agree on which links we will record, such as business objective to requirement, requirement to design, requirement to test, and requirement to change request. We also decide the level of detail, so a requirement is not split so finely that the matrix becomes unmanageable. We pick where the links live, whether a spreadsheet or a requirements tool, and who updates each link. We set a review point, such as at every approved change and at each release gate. The tradeoff of tracing too much is effort: every link needs maintenance, and if the team cannot keep up, the links go stale and the matrix becomes misleading. So I would keep only the links that answer the questions stakeholders actually ask, like what breaks if this changes.
rubricPoints: States which link types the strategy records, such as objective to requirement and requirement to test
Explains the chosen granularity and why it must be manageable
Names where links are stored and who is responsible for updating them
Identifies a real limit or tradeoff, such as maintenance effort or stale links

suggested.rationale: Explaining which links to set and why is the core skill, and no listed mission or planned engine covers requirements traceability.

lessons.plain: Before a team gathers requirements, someone should write down how that work will be run: who is affected by the project and how much they matter, who does which job, how the team will draw out what people need, how it will check those needs make sense, and who has to say yes before they count. That written agreement is a requirements management plan. It is short, it is specific to this project, and it prevents later arguments about who decided what and when. Think of it as the rules of the game, written before the first move.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project has ten stakeholders, and two of them disagree about what a feature should do. Before any analysis starts, what would you put in writing so the team knows who settles the disagreement and how the decision gets recorded?
lessons.teach:
A requirements management plan is a written agreement, made early in a project, that sets out how requirements will be gathered, analyzed, approved and kept under control. It answers three questions in particular. First, who are the stakeholders, meaning the people or groups who are affected by the work or can influence it? Second, who is responsible for which activity? Third, which methods will be used for elicitation (drawing requirements out of people through interviews, workshops, observation or document review), for analysis (checking that requirements are complete, consistent and testable), and for approval (getting a named decision-maker to accept them)?

Why it works: requirements conflict when different people hold different pictures of the same product. The plan forces those pictures into the open before work starts. Each stakeholder is listed with their interest and influence, so the team knows who must be consulted and who only needs to be informed. A responsibility matrix, a table that lists each activity against each person and marks who does it, who approves it, who is consulted and who is informed, removes guessing about who writes, who signs off, and who can be overruled.

Worked example: a clinic is building a booking app. Step 1: the analyst lists stakeholders, including front-desk staff (high interest, high influence), two doctors (high influence), an IT contractor (medium) and patients (indirect). Step 2: the plan names the analyst as author, the operations manager as the single approver for scope, and the doctors as approvers for clinical workflow. Step 3: workshops are chosen for front-desk rules and interviews for the doctors. Step 4: approval is recorded as a named sign-off in the change log, not as a hallway agreement.

Common mistake: naming 'all stakeholders' as approvers, or leaving approval out entirely, so nobody can say whether a change was agreed.

Consequence: when a doctor later asks for a new feature, the team can point to the plan, see that the doctor is not the scope approver, and route the request correctly instead of quietly absorbing it into the build.

questions.prompt: A regional transit authority is writing a requirements management plan for a fare-card top-up website. Step 1: the analyst lists stakeholders, including the fare-systems manager (high interest, high influence), bus drivers (indirect, low influence), a payments vendor (medium influence) and daily riders (high interest, low influence). Step 2: the plan names the analyst as author and the fare-systems manager as the single approver for scope. Step 3: the analyst picks interviews for the fare-systems manager and a short online survey for riders, who are spread across the city. Step 4 is missing and has not been written yet: it should state how approval of the agreed requirements is recorded. Which completion of Step 4 fits the method this plan follows?
choices: Accept approval as a verbal agreement recorded at the next team meeting.
Record the approval as a named sign-off in the change log, given by the fare-systems manager as the single scope approver.
Make all four stakeholders approvers so that no group is left out of the decision.
Leave approval out of the plan until testing, when riders can react to a working build.
questions.why: The method calls for a named decision-maker and a recorded sign-off, which is what the first completion provides, while the other three are the common mistakes of listing everyone as approver, omitting approval, or relying on an unrecorded agreement.

questions.prompt: A small charity is writing its requirements management plan for a volunteer scheduling tool. Which planning artifact lists each activity against each person and marks who does it, who approves it, who is consulted and who is informed?
choices: A stakeholder register that rates each person's interest and influence
A completeness checklist for analysis
A change log that records named sign-offs
A responsibility matrix
questions.why: A responsibility matrix is the table that pairs activities with people and marks each person's role, which is different from a stakeholder list, a change log or an analysis checklist.

questions.prompt: A team lets every stakeholder count as an approver for the scope of a new reporting feature. Later, one stakeholder asks for an extra report. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: Elicitation methods are replaced by document review for the rest of the project.
Nobody can say whether the change was agreed, so the extra report is absorbed quietly into the build.
The request is routed to a single scope approver, as the plan intended.
The analyst is automatically named the approver and must sign off every change.
questions.why: When approval is given to everyone, there is no single decision-maker to point to, so an unagreed change slips into the build without a recorded decision.

questions.prompt: A university lab is planning a sample-tracking system. Stakeholders include a lab manager (high interest, high influence), two postdoc researchers (high interest, low influence), an external equipment vendor (medium influence) and grant funders who only read final reports. Which elicitation approach best suits the postdocs' detailed daily workflow?
choices: Ask the funders to sign off on the workflow before any elicitation starts.
Keep the postdocs as informed-only stakeholders with no elicitation.
Use the vendor's manual as the sole source of requirements.
Observe their daily workflow, then follow up with a short interview.
questions.why: Observation paired with interviews draws requirements out of the people who do the work, whereas the other options either give approval to the wrong people, rely on a vendor document, or skip elicitation for people who need it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a requirements management plan must say about stakeholders, roles and responsibilities, and elicitation, analysis and approval methods, and name one limit or tradeoff of writing this plan before the work begins.
lessons.modelAnswer: A requirements management plan sets the ground rules before requirements work starts. It lists the stakeholders and how much each one matters, usually by interest and influence, so we know who must be consulted and who only needs updates. It assigns roles with a responsibility matrix, so every activity has one author and one named approver, and nobody is left guessing who can overrule whom. It states which elicitation methods we will use for each group, such as workshops for front-desk staff and interviews for senior clinicians, and how we will analyze and approve what comes back. The main limit is that the plan is written from what we know on day one. Stakeholders and influence shift as the project learns more, so the plan needs a review point, or it becomes a document nobody follows.
rubricPoints: Names the stakeholders and their interest and influence, not just a list of job titles
Assigns roles and responsibilities, including a single named approver for each decision
Chooses elicitation and analysis methods that fit each stakeholder group
Explains approval as a recorded sign-off, and notes that the plan needs review as understanding changes

suggested.rationale: No listed OpsForge mission or planned engine covers writing a requirements plan, and explaining its parts back to a teammate is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: When a project's requirements change after work has started, someone has to decide how each change is asked for, checked, approved and recorded. A change-control method is the set of steps and rules for doing that. A standard protocol is a repeatable routine inside that method, such as a fixed request form, a review meeting on a set schedule, or a rule about who signs off. Planning this in advance and writing it into the change management plan means the team doesn't invent a process every time a stakeholder wants something different. Think of it as the house rules for a shared kitchen: everyone knows how to ask for an ingredient to be swapped and who says yes.
lessons.guessPrompt: A stakeholder emails the project lead on day 40 asking for a feature that the team has already designed differently. What would you want agreed before day 1 so that this request does not derail the project?
lessons.teach:
A requirement is a stated need the solution must meet. A baseline is an agreed set of requirements frozen at a point in time, and changes after that point go through change control, which is the formal process for proposing, assessing, deciding on and recording a change. The change management plan is the document that states which change-control method the project will use and which standard protocols apply. A protocol here means a repeatable routine, such as a fixed change request form, a set review cadence, or a rule about who holds decision rights.

Why it works: a change looks small in isolation, but requirements link to other requirements, designs, tests and budgets. Impact analysis, the step of tracing a proposed change through those links to see what it touches, is what makes the decision informed. Change control makes that trace happen every time, instead of relying on memory.

Worked example. A sponsor asks that a fleet alert threshold move from 80 to 90 kilometres per hour. Step 1: log a change request with an ID and the reason. Step 2: the analyst traces the linked requirements, the alert test cases and the dispatch training material, and estimates effort. Step 3: the change control board, a named group with decision rights, reviews it in its weekly slot. Step 4: it is approved, with a note on schedule impact. Step 5: the baseline is updated to a new version and affected parties are told.

Common mistake: agreeing to a change in a corridor conversation and updating the system without a record. The consequence is that tests still check the old threshold, the training material disagrees with the live system, and nobody can say which version was approved.

A change-control method that is written down, with a clear route from request to decision, is what keeps a project's requirements trustworthy.

questions.prompt: A regional pharmacy chain has a stock-tracking system with a baseline of approved requirements. A store manager asks that the expiry warning window change from 30 days to 45 days. Step 1: the request is logged with an ID and the reason (short-dated stock is being discarded too early). Step 2: the analyst traces the change to the linked requirements for reorder rules, the expiry-report test cases and the staff guide on handling warnings, and estimates the effort. Step 3 is missing from this trace and must be filled in before the change can be decided: the change is put to the change control board, a named group with decision rights, at its scheduled review. Step 4: the board approves the change and records the schedule impact. Step 5: the baseline is versioned and affected staff are told. Which action belongs in the missing step, given that the board's review is the decision point?
choices: Start configuring the new 45-day window in the live system so the store can use it while the board is still considering it.
Skip the board and have the store manager approve the change by email, since the change affects only one store.
Present the traced impact to the board at its scheduled review so it can decide on an informed basis.
Update the expiry-report test cases to 45 days so the tests match the change before any decision is made.
questions.why: The missing step is the formal decision by the named board using the impact analysis, which is what separates an approved, recorded change from an untracked one.

questions.prompt: In a change-control context, what is a baseline?
choices: An agreed set of requirements frozen at a point in time, after which changes go through formal change control.
The estimated cost of implementing all requirements, used to set the project budget.
The first draft of the requirements document, which is replaced as soon as stakeholders comment on it.
A list of every stakeholder who may ask for changes during a project.
questions.why: A baseline is defined as an agreed, frozen set of requirements, and the defining feature is that later changes must pass through change control.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm is building a parcel-tracking portal and a client asks, mid-build, to change the delivery-status update from hourly to every fifteen minutes. The firm's change management plan must specify protocols. Which protocol best fits the need to make sure this request is judged with its knock-on effects in view?
choices: A rule that the developer may decide any change under a set cost limit, without review.
A promise that changes will be batched into the final release, with no earlier review.
A verbal sign-off from the client's operations lead during a weekly call.
A standard change request form that asks for the reason and triggers a traced impact analysis before decision.
questions.why: A fixed change request form that triggers impact analysis is the protocol that makes the trace through linked requirements, tests and budgets happen each time.

questions.prompt: A product team lets a developer edit acceptance criteria directly in a shared cloud tracker whenever the developer finds them unclear, with no change request raised. Which outcome is the most direct consequence of this practice for a running system?
choices: The team can no longer show which version of the criteria was approved, and tests may still check the old criteria.
The client is charged a fixed fee for each edit, which removes the need for change control.
The tracker will automatically run every test again, so no defect can slip through.
The project's baseline is strengthened because the criteria stay more accurate than before.
questions.why: Editing criteria without a change record means approval history is lost and test cases can drift from the agreed requirements, which is the risk change control exists to prevent.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never run change control how the project should handle a late change request, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would tell them the late request goes through the change-control method already written into our change management plan, not straight to a developer. First we log it with an ID and a reason, then we do impact analysis: trace the linked requirements, tests and design to see what the change touches and what it costs. The change control board then decides on its normal schedule, approving, rejecting or deferring. If approved, we version the baseline and tell the people affected. The tradeoff is speed. A formal route adds days, so an urgent safety fix may need an expedited path, and the plan should define when that is allowed. Without that exception, people bypass the process and the record is lost.
rubricPoints: Describes change control as a documented route from request to decision
Mentions impact analysis that traces linked requirements, tests and design
Names decision rights, such as a change control board
States a limit or tradeoff, such as added time or the need for an expedited path
Notes that an approved change updates the baseline and its version

suggested.rationale: An exam-style situation where the learner picks the right change route and justifies it adds more than any listed mission or planned engine.

lessons.plain: Document control is the set of rules for how project documents are named, stored, numbered, approved and updated, so everyone knows which copy of a requirement is the current one. Traceability is the ability to follow a requirement forward to the design, tests and delivered feature it produced, and backward to the business need that justified it. Before requirements work starts, a business analyst chooses the document-control methods that make both possible, much as a library picks its cataloguing system before the first book arrives. The choice is made once, written into the plan, and applied to every requirement that follows.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has 200 requirements in a shared folder, with files named final, final2 and final_REAL. A tester says a test failed against a requirement that no longer matches what was approved. Which one planning decision would have prevented this confusion most directly, and why?
lessons.teach:
A requirement is a statement of a need or condition the solution must meet. Requirements traceability means linking each requirement to where it came from (its source, such as a business objective or stakeholder), to what depends on it (design items, tests, code), and back again. A traceability matrix is the table that records these links. Document control is the set of methods that governs each document: a unique identifier, an owner, a version number, an approval status, and a rule for who may change it. A version is a numbered state of a document. A baseline is a version that has been formally approved and that later changes must be measured against.

Why it works: links and versions only mean something if each item has one stable identifier and one approved current version. Without those, a link points at a moving target.

Worked example. Requirement REQ-042 says a dispatcher sees a vehicle position within 5 seconds. Step 1: the analyst gives it the identifier REQ-042 in the requirements register. Step 2: the register records its source as objective BO-3, reduce late deliveries. Step 3: the sponsor approves it at version 1.0, which becomes the baseline. Step 4: the design item and test case TC-118 are linked to REQ-042. Step 5: a change request proposes 10 seconds; it is approved, and the requirement moves to version 1.1 with the change logged. Step 6: the matrix shows that TC-118 must be updated before release.

Common mistake: editing the requirement in place, or emailing attachments, so two copies disagree and nobody can say which was approved. Consequence in a running system: if TC-118 still tests the 5-second target after the agreed change, the release can pass its tests while missing the approved target.

A traceable requirement is one with a stable identifier, a recorded source, and a single approved version that every linked item points to.

questions.prompt: A hospital pharmacy project records REQ-17: a pharmacist sees a ward stock count updated within 2 minutes of a dispense. Step 1: the analyst gives it the identifier REQ-17 in the requirements register. Step 2: the register records its source as objective BO-8, cut stock-outs on wards. Step 3: the medication manager approves it at version 1.0, which becomes the baseline. Step 4: test case TC-40 and the screen design item are linked to REQ-17. Step 5: a change request proposes 4 minutes instead, and it is approved. Step 6: [missing step]. Step 7: the matrix shows TC-40 must be updated before go-live. Which completes the missing Step 6?
choices: The requirement is given a new identifier, REQ-17B, and the old REQ-17 is deleted from the register.
The requirement moves to version 1.1 with the change logged, and 1.0 stays unchanged as the baseline.
The approved change is emailed to the ward managers as an attachment so they have the new wording.
The team edits the 1.0 text in place and keeps the number 1.0, noting the change in a comment.
questions.why: An approved change creates a new numbered version with the change logged, while the approved baseline version stays intact so links and comparisons remain meaningful.

questions.prompt: Which set of properties makes a requirement traceable under this course's method?
choices: A detailed description, a named author, and a due date
A recorded source only, since the identifier can change between drafts
A unique title, a list of test cases, and a signed sponsor email
A stable identifier, a recorded source, and one approved version that every linked item points to
questions.why: The teaching text defines a traceable requirement by a stable identifier, a recorded source, and a single approved version that every linked item points to.

questions.prompt: A team sends a requirement to a vendor as an emailed attachment, and the vendor edits it and returns a second copy. What problem does this create?
choices: Two copies can disagree and no one can say which copy was approved, so links may point to unapproved wording.
The vendor's file is too large for the requirements register to store.
The sponsor must approve every email, which slows the project down.
The requirement automatically loses its identifier when it leaves the register.
questions.why: Copies that drift apart make it impossible to tell which wording was approved, which is the common mistake the teaching text warns about.

questions.prompt: A school timetabling project has requirement REQ-09 at baseline version 2.0. A team member wants to change it. What should happen first?
choices: A change request is raised and, if approved, a new version 2.1 is created with the change logged before linked tests are updated.
The team gives REQ-09 a new identifier so the old tests stop pointing to it.
The baseline is deleted so the change can be made freely.
The team overwrites the 2.0 text and keeps the version number so existing links stay valid.
questions.why: A baseline is changed only through an approved change that produces a new version with the change logged, and the traceability matrix then shows which linked items need updating.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, why document-control methods such as identifiers, versions and approval states should be chosen before requirements work starts, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you would recommend for a small team.
lessons.modelAnswer: Document-control methods decide how each requirement gets a stable identifier, a version number, an owner and an approval status. If we choose them after work has started, earlier requirements will already be scattered across emails and files, and the links we build will point at copies nobody can verify. Choosing them up front means every later link, test and change refers to one approved version. The tradeoff for a small team is overhead. A full register with formal approvals and a change log can feel heavy for a dozen requirements, so I would keep the same identifiers and version rules but accept a lighter approval step, and document that choice in the plan so the team knows where the rigour is and is not.
rubricPoints: Explains that methods are chosen before work starts so identifiers and versions stay stable.
Connects stable identifiers and versions to reliable traceability links.
Names a concrete limit or tradeoff, such as overhead or slower approval for small teams.
Shows the choice is recorded in the plan so it can be applied consistently.

suggested.rationale: A situation where the learner must pick document-control rules for a realistic requirements set adds more than reading definitions, and no listed mission or planned engine covers requirements documents directly.

lessons.plain: Before anyone builds anything, the people who will use or pay for the work need to agree on two things: how success will be measured in business terms, and what a finished piece of work must do before they accept it. A business metric is a number the organisation already cares about, such as orders delivered on time or refunds processed per week. Acceptance criteria are the specific conditions a piece of work must meet before the people who asked for it will sign off. Agreeing these together with stakeholders, rather than writing them alone in a document, makes sure the numbers and conditions reflect what the business actually needs.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team says their new scheduling feature is done because the developers finished coding it and the tests pass. Why might the business still be unhappy with it, and what should have been agreed before work began to prevent that?
lessons.teach:
A stakeholder is anyone with an interest in the outcome, such as a dispatcher, a finance lead, or the sponsor who funds the work. A business metric is a measurable result the organisation cares about, stated in business terms. A baseline is the current value of that metric before any change, and a target is the value the stakeholders agree the change should reach by a stated date. Acceptance criteria are testable conditions that a requirement or solution must satisfy before the business accepts it. Each criterion should name a condition, an action, and an observable result.
