This works collaboratively because the people who feel the pain know which numbers matter, and the sponsor must agree what success means. The business analyst runs the workshops, records disagreements, and obtains sign-off. A shared, measured target stops a team from declaring victory on output alone.

Worked example: a courier company wants faster driver assignment. The baseline is 22 minutes from order placed to driver assigned, averaged over last month. Stakeholders agree the target is under 10 minutes for 90 percent of orders within three months. One acceptance criterion reads: given an evening peak order, when the dispatch rule runs, then a driver is assigned within 10 minutes for at least 90 percent of orders in the pilot sample. The metric names the measure, the baseline gives the starting point, and the criterion gives a test.

Common mistake: writing criteria as vague adjectives such as fast or user-friendly. No one can test them, and each stakeholder reads them differently.

In a running system, a metric chosen only by engineers, such as average server response time, can look healthy while drivers still wait, because it never measured the business outcome.

Business metrics and acceptance criteria are agreed together, compared against a baseline, and written so that a test can confirm them.

questions.prompt: A hotel wants faster room turnaround after guest checkout. The business analyst has done three steps. Step 1: name the metric as the time from guest checkout to the room being marked ready for the next guest. Step 2: record the baseline, which is 38 minutes on average across last month's checkouts. Step 3: agree the target with the housekeeping lead and the sponsor: under 25 minutes for 85 percent of checkouts within two months. Step 4, which is missing: write one acceptance criterion that a tester could check against the pilot sample. Which completion of step 4 is correct?
choices: Given a guest checkout at midday, when the housekeeper marks the room Ready in the app, then the status shows Ready within 25 minutes for at least 85 percent of checkouts in the pilot sample.
The average checkout-to-ready time over the month is 38 minutes, which is recorded as the baseline.
Housekeeping is fast and guests are happy with the room when they arrive at it.
Average housekeeper active minutes per shift fall below the level recorded last quarter.
questions.why: The correct criterion names a condition (midday checkout), an action (marking Ready), and an observable result (status within 25 minutes for 85 percent of cases), so a tester can confirm it, while the other choices are vague, measure the wrong thing, or restate the baseline.

questions.prompt: A regional bank's loan team records that the average time from application received to decision was 9 days last quarter. Before any change is made, what is this 9-day figure called?
choices: A baseline
A business metric
A target
An acceptance criterion
questions.why: A baseline is the current value of a metric before any change, and the 9-day average is that starting value, whereas a target is the agreed future value.

questions.prompt: An engineer on a parcel-locker project chooses average API response time, 120 milliseconds, as the only success measure. Users keep reporting they cannot find a free locker within a reasonable wait. What is the main weakness of this choice?
choices: Milliseconds are the wrong unit and the team should use seconds instead.
The measure was chosen by engineers and does not capture the business outcome, so the project could report success while users still struggle.
A baseline cannot be recorded for a response time, so the project cannot start.
Acceptance criteria must always use calendar months, so response time is not allowed.
questions.why: A metric chosen only by engineers can look healthy while the business result, here users finding a locker, stays poor, because it never measured that outcome.

questions.prompt: A university library is testing a self-checkout kiosk. Which of these is written as an acceptance criterion that a tester could confirm or reject?
choices: The kiosk is reliable and rarely causes problems at the desk.
Given a student with a valid card and one book, when the student scans the book at the kiosk, then the loan receipt prints within 15 seconds for at least 95 percent of attempts in a one-week trial.
Students should be happy with the kiosk after a few visits.
The kiosk should be easy for students to use.
questions.why: Only the last option names a condition, an action, and an observable result with a measurable threshold, while the others use vague adjectives that no tester can check consistently.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has just joined the project why business metrics and acceptance criteria should be agreed with stakeholders before design starts, and name one limit or tradeoff of doing it this way.
lessons.modelAnswer: Agreeing metrics and acceptance criteria before design starts gives everyone one definition of done in business terms. The team can then design toward a target that the sponsor and the users have already accepted, instead of discovering mid-build that they wanted something else. Each criterion should be testable, with a baseline to measure against, so that acceptance is a check rather than an argument. The main tradeoff is time: getting stakeholders to agree takes workshops and follow-up, and early agreement can feel slow. Also, criteria agreed early may need revisiting when the business changes, so they should be kept under change control and not treated as fixed forever. Naming that limit openly is part of a sound plan.
rubricPoints: Metrics and acceptance criteria are agreed with stakeholders before design, giving one shared definition of done.
Each criterion must be testable and tied to a measurable business outcome, with a baseline where useful.
A real limitation is named, such as the time cost of consensus or the need to revise criteria as the business changes.
The answer uses plain terms and does not rely on vague words such as fast or user-friendly.

suggested.rationale: Choosing and justifying metrics and criteria with stakeholders is a judgment skill best tested by explaining it to a teammate, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it directly.

lessons.plain: Elicitation means drawing out what people actually need from a project, rather than waiting for them to describe it perfectly. A requirement is a condition or capability a finished solution must have. Business analysts use several ways to find requirements: talking one-to-one with people, watching them work, reading existing paperwork, and bringing groups together to compare views. For every requirement, they also record where it came from and why it matters, so that the team can later explain, question, or change it. This lesson covers those skills, with no software steps.
lessons.guessPrompt: A stakeholder says we need reports faster. Before you learn any technique, what single piece of information would you most want to know so that this becomes a useful requirement, and why?
lessons.teach:
Elicitation means drawing out requirements from people and sources, rather than waiting for them to arrive fully formed. A requirement is a condition or capability that a solution must meet. Individual techniques work with one person or one source at a time. An interview is a structured conversation with one stakeholder. Observation means watching someone do their real work, sometimes called shadowing. Document analysis means reading existing procedures, forms, or reports to find rules already in use. A questionnaire is a written set of questions sent to many people. Group techniques bring several stakeholders together. A facilitated workshop is a guided session where people agree on needs together. A focus group gathers a set of users to react to ideas. Brainstorming generates many ideas quickly, and the group sorts them afterwards. Why this works: people often cannot state what they need, and each group describes the same need differently. Using more than one technique and comparing results exposes gaps and conflicts.

Two attributes make a requirement traceable. Origin records where it came from: a named stakeholder, a document, a regulation, or an observed workaround. Rationale records why it exists, meaning the business problem or goal it serves. Without these, nobody can later judge whether a requirement can be changed or dropped.

Worked example. A dispatcher says show me the trucks within five kilometres. Step 1: record the words as stated. Step 2: set origin to the dispatcher, captured in an interview on a named date. Step 3: ask why. The dispatcher reassigns nearby drivers to urgent pickups within minutes. Step 4: record rationale as reducing the time taken to reassign urgent pickups. Step 5: a later workshop with operations finds the five-kilometre figure is a guess, so the requirement is revised, with a note of who confirmed the change.

Common mistake: recording the proposed solution as the requirement, such as add a map widget, and losing the underlying need.

Consequence: when two requirements with no recorded rationale conflict during scope decisions, the team cannot tell which one serves the goal, so the loudest voice usually wins.

questions.prompt: A city library wants to capture a request to renew loans online. Step 1: record the member's words as stated: 'Let me renew my books from home.' Step 2: set origin to a named member, captured in an interview on 3 March. Step 3: ask why. The member explains that they currently ask a neighbour to renew for them, and the renewal fails whenever the neighbour is away. Step 4 is missing from this record. Which entry completes Step 4 correctly?
choices: Delete the entry, because a request that depends on a neighbour is a personal arrangement rather than a requirement.
Record the rationale as reducing members' dependence on third parties to keep their loans active.
Record the requirement as 'add an online renewal button to the catalogue page', because the proposed solution shows what is needed.
Record the origin a second time as the library's catalogue system, so the source is visible from both sides.
questions.why: Rationale records the business problem the requirement serves, and the member's explanation about relying on a neighbour points to that problem, while the other choices either record a solution or lose the need.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm wants to learn how warehouse pickers actually handle damaged-item returns, including informal shortcuts that staff may not mention in an interview. Which elicitation technique best fits this need?
choices: A questionnaire sent to all pickers asking them to describe the process.
A focus group where pickers react to a proposed returns screen.
A brainstorming session in which pickers suggest ideas for returns.
Observation, where the analyst watches pickers do their real work.
questions.why: Observation records real work as it happens, so it can surface informal shortcuts that people may not describe when asked directly.

questions.prompt: In a workshop for a regional hospital's scheduling team, a participant's need is recorded as 'add a red warning banner to the appointment screen'. What is the main risk of recording it this way?
choices: The banner will be too expensive to build for the hospital's budget.
Workshop participants will be unable to vote on the banner's colour.
The requirement will automatically be traced to the wrong regulation.
The underlying need is lost, so nobody can judge whether the banner is the best way to meet it.
questions.why: Recording a proposed solution in place of the requirement loses the underlying need, which is needed to evaluate alternatives or revise the requirement later.

questions.prompt: Two requirements for a parcel-tracking system conflict during a scope decision. Neither has a recorded origin or rationale. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: The team can judge from the origins which requirement is more regulated and drops the other.
The conflict is resolved by the tracking system's default settings.
The system automatically keeps both requirements and builds them in sequence.
The team cannot tell which requirement serves the goal, so the decision tends to favour whichever stakeholder argues most forcefully.
questions.why: Without rationale the team has no basis for comparing the requirements against the goal, so the loudest voice usually decides the scope.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between an individual and a group elicitation technique. Give one example of each, then name one limit of relying on interviews alone and how you would reduce that limit.
lessons.modelAnswer: Individual techniques, such as interviews or observation, work with one person or source at a time. They let you probe deeply and see real work, but they can miss what other stakeholders need, and one person may not describe their work completely. Group techniques, such as a facilitated workshop, bring several stakeholders together so they can agree on needs and surface conflicts early. The limit of interviews alone is that the answers reflect one person's view and memory. To reduce that, I would cross-check interview findings with a second source, such as observation or document analysis, and take conflicting points to a workshop. For each requirement I would record its origin and rationale so the team can see who said it and why it matters.
rubricPoints: Defines individual techniques as one-to-one or single-source work, with at least one example
Defines group techniques as multi-stakeholder sessions, with at least one example
Names a concrete limit of interviews, such as single-person bias or incomplete recall
Explains that origin records the source and rationale records the reason it matters

suggested.rationale: Choosing and justifying the right technique for raw stakeholder input is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario, which no existing mission covers directly.

lessons.plain: Requirements analysis is the work of taking raw wishes and comments from people and turning them into a clear, connected picture. You break a big need into smaller pieces, work out which pieces must be finished before others can start, check where the solution meets other systems or people, and sketch how information and steps flow. Think of a restaurant kitchen. Before anyone cooks, someone maps which dish depends on which ingredient, which station hands off to which, and what gets written on each order ticket. Analysts do the same for a system so the team builds the right things in the right order.
lessons.guessPrompt: A customer says: 'The monthly statement must show the final invoice total.' Before any teaching, list two things that would have to exist or be agreed before anyone could calculate that total, and say why you picked each one.
lessons.teach:
Decomposition means splitting one requirement into smaller parts that can each be checked. A dependency is a link where one requirement cannot be completed or tested until another is in place. Dependency analysis is the act of finding and recording those links. Interface analysis looks at each point where your solution exchanges data or actions with another system, person, or process, and records the direction, format, and timing of that exchange. A data model describes the things the solution must store and how they relate to each other. A process model shows the steps, decisions, and handoffs that turn an input into an outcome, often as a flow diagram. Together these tools expose what a flat wish list hides.

Worked example. The requirement is: show the final invoice total on the statement. Step one, decompose it: capture order lines, apply the discount, apply the tax rate, round to cents, then print. Step two, find dependencies: the total depends on discount and tax; the statement depends on the total. Step three, analyze interfaces: the tax rate comes from a pricing service, and the statement printer receives the total. Record the format and update timing of each. Step four, model data: an invoice has many lines, and each line has a quantity and unit price. Step five, model the process: calculate lines, discount, tax, round, publish. Each step now has a named owner and a checkable output.

Common mistake: treating the list as independent items, so the team builds the statement before tax rules are settled and assumes the tax service returns rates in a format nobody wrote down.

Consequence: when the pricing service changes its rate format, the statement fails in production, and nobody knew the statement depended on that interface.

Elaborated requirements, with their links and interfaces visible, are what let a team plan, test, and change safely.

questions.prompt: A small dental clinic wants its scheduling system to send each patient a text reminder 24 hours before their appointment. The team decomposed the requirement into four parts: read tomorrow's appointments, check each patient's mobile number, build the reminder text, and send it through the SMS gateway (a outside messaging provider that accepts texts from the clinic's system). Dependencies were recorded: sending depends on the appointment time and on a valid mobile number. For the interface with the scheduling system, the team recorded that it exports appointment times nightly as a timestamp in a fixed format, pushed from scheduling to the reminder job. For the interface with the SMS gateway, the team recorded that the clinic's system sends the message text and the patient's number to the gateway, in a fixed format, at the moment of sending. The gateway also returns a delivery receipt for each message, but nobody has recorded that return exchange yet. Which entry completes the interface record for the receipt?
choices: Direction: none, because a sent message needs no record of whether it arrived
Direction: gateway to the patient's phone; format: plain text; timing: at the appointment time
Direction: gateway back to the clinic system; format: a status code tied to each message ID; timing: arrives shortly after each send attempt
Direction: clinic system to gateway; format: a yearly account summary; timing: once a year
questions.why: Interface analysis requires recording the direction, format, and timing of every exchange, and the receipt is a real exchange flowing back from the gateway to the clinic system, so its record must follow the same three checks.

questions.prompt: In a warehouse picking app, the requirement 'print the pick label' cannot be tested until the bin location data has been loaded into the app. Which term describes the link between these two items?
choices: A dependency, because the label cannot be completed or tested until the bin data is in place
A data model, because it describes how bin locations are stored
A process model, because it shows the steps of picking an item
A decomposition, because the label is split into smaller checkable parts
questions.why: A dependency is a link where one requirement cannot be completed or tested until another is in place, which is exactly the relationship described between the label and the bin data.

questions.prompt: A public library's loan system calculates each due date by reading a loan period from the catalog service. The team never wrote down that the catalog service returns the loan period in days, and a catalog update switched it to weeks without notice. What is the most likely consequence for the running system?
choices: Loans are rejected at the desk, because the system detects every change in format automatically
The catalog service stops working until the library team writes its interface record
Due dates are unaffected, because a due date is stored independently of the loan period
Loans are issued with due dates far off from what the library intended, and nobody notices because the link to the catalog was never recorded
questions.why: The loan system depends on an interface whose format was never recorded, so a silent change in units produces wrong due dates in production with no visible signal, which is the consequence of skipping interface analysis.

questions.prompt: A volunteer group organizes weekend food-bank shifts. A business analyst is asked to produce a process model for sign-up. Which description best matches what a process model shows?
choices: A list of the database tables that hold volunteer names, shift dates, and contact details, with the relationships between them
The steps, decisions, and handoffs that turn a volunteer's request to join a shift into a confirmed place, often drawn as a flow diagram
The format and timing of the messages the sign-up page sends to the email provider
A set of volunteer roles grouped by how many hours each person can give per month
questions.why: A process model shows the steps, decisions, and handoffs that turn an input into an outcome, often as a flow diagram, whereas the database tables describe a data model and the message format describes an interface.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a new teammate what dependency analysis, interface analysis, and data or process modeling each add when you elaborate a requirement, and name one limit or tradeoff of building detailed models before stakeholders have agreed on scope.
lessons.modelAnswer: Dependency analysis tells us which requirements block others, so we know the order of delivery and what breaks if one slips. Interface analysis records each point where we exchange data or actions with another system or person, including direction, format, and timing, so integration risks surface early. Data modeling shows the things we must store and how they relate, which keeps the team from inventing conflicting definitions. Process modeling shows the steps and handoffs, which reveals gaps like a step with no owner. The tradeoff is that detailed models take time and can give false confidence. If the scope is still moving, a detailed model may need redrawing, so I would keep models light until stakeholders agree on the boundary, then deepen them for the parts that are about to be built.
rubricPoints: Explains dependency analysis as finding which requirements must precede others, affecting sequence and risk.
Explains interface analysis as recording exchanges with other systems or people, including format and timing.
Describes data or process modeling as showing stored things and steps, revealing gaps or conflicts.
Names a concrete limit or tradeoff, such as effort or false confidence when scope is unsettled.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission asks learners to decompose and model requirements, so an exam-style scenario to reason through adds the most.

lessons.plain: When a team is handed a long wish list of features, not all of them can be built, and some may not be worth building. Evaluating options means looking at each candidate requirement and asking whether it earns its place. You compare it with the other candidates using criteria the stakeholders agreed on, such as how much value it brings, how costly it is, how risky it is, and how well it fits the goals. Based on that comparison you accept it now, defer it to a later release, or reject it. This lesson covers the common ways to make that call and how to write the decision down so it can be explained later.
lessons.guessPrompt: A product team has twelve requested features and budget for only five. Before reading anything, how would you decide which five to keep, and what would you need to know about each one?
lessons.teach:
A requirement is a stated need that the solution must meet. An option is a candidate requirement or capability being considered for the next release. Decision criteria are the measures you agree on in advance, such as business value, cost to deliver, risk, and fit with goals. A weighted score multiplies each criterion's rating by its agreed weight and adds the results, so one number can rank the options while the weights stay visible. Accept means the requirement enters the current scope. Defer means it is valid but waits for a later release. Reject means it is set aside with a recorded reason.

Why it works: making the criteria and weights explicit before scoring stops the loudest stakeholder from winning by default and lets everyone see why a choice was made.

Worked example. Three requests: X, a report export; Y, single sign-on login; Z, dark mode. Weights: value 60 percent, ease of delivery 40 percent, where a request that is cheap to build scores high on ease. Ratings out of 5: X has value 4 and ease 2; Y has value 3 and ease 5; Z has value 5 and ease 1. Step one, X scores 0.6 times 4 plus 0.4 times 2, which is 3.2. Step two, Y scores 0.6 times 3 plus 0.4 times 5, which is 3.8. Step three, Z scores 0.6 times 5 plus 0.4 times 1, which is 3.4. Ranking: Y, then Z, then X. If capacity fits only Y and Z, you accept those two and defer X with its reason written down.

Common mistake: rejecting a low-scoring requirement that another accepted requirement depends on. Check dependencies before setting anything aside, because a rejected prerequisite leaves an accepted feature unable to work.

The score informs the decision; it does not replace the stakeholder agreement that stands behind the criteria and weights.

questions.prompt: A clinic team scores three requests for its patient portal. The agreed criteria are value to patients at 50 percent, risk at 30 percent (a low-risk request scores high), and cost to build at 20 percent (a cheap request scores high). Ratings out of 5: option A (appointment reminder texts) has value 4, risk 3, cost 4. Option B (printed visit summaries) has value 2, risk 5, cost 3. Option C (bulk record import) has value 5, risk 2, cost 2. Step one: the value contribution for C is 0.5 times 5, which is 2.5. Step two: the risk contribution for C is 0.3 times 2, which is 0.6. Step three is missing. Step four: add the three contributions to get C's total score.
choices: Multiply the total score by the cost weight of 0.2 before adding.
Cost contribution is 0.2 times 5, which is 1.0, using the value rating.
Rank C against A and B before computing any contributions.
Cost contribution is 0.2 times 2, which is 0.4.
questions.why: Each criterion's contribution is its agreed weight times the option's rating on that criterion, so C's cost contribution is 0.2 times its cost rating of 2, giving 0.4.

questions.prompt: A payroll team has a valid request that scores well but cannot fit into the current release. What is the correct status to give it, and what must be recorded?
choices: Hold it indefinitely with no status until capacity is known.
Reject it, and record that it was dropped from the project.
Accept it into the current scope and move other work out to make room.
Defer it: it stays valid and waits for a later release, with the reason written down.
questions.why: Defer means the requirement is valid but waits for a later release, and the reason should be recorded, which is exactly what the choice describes.

questions.prompt: A team rejected a low-scoring request R without checking anything else. Later, an accepted request S stopped working because it needed R's underlying function. Which mistake caused this?
choices: Accepted requirements should never be scored alongside rejected ones.
The weights were set too high on the value criterion.
Dependencies were not checked before R was set aside.
Rejected requests should always be given a score of zero.
questions.why: Rejecting a prerequisite without checking dependencies leaves an accepted feature unable to work, which is the common mistake the text warns about.

questions.prompt: A product owner says the option with the highest weighted score must be accepted automatically, because the number settles the question and the stakeholder agreement about criteria no longer matters. What is the best response?
choices: Refuse to compute scores at all, since weights make the result unreliable.
The score informs the decision, but the stakeholder agreement behind the criteria and weights still stands.
Accept the top score only after the criteria and weights are re-chosen by the product owner alone.
Agree, since a computed score should always override earlier stakeholder agreements.
questions.why: The text says the score informs the decision and does not replace the stakeholder agreement that stands behind the criteria and weights.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide which requests to accept, defer, or reject when the budget covers only some of them. Name one limitation of the method you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would first agree with the sponsor and main stakeholders on the criteria and their weights, such as business value, cost to deliver, risk, and alignment with the goals, and write them down. Then I would rate each requirement against each criterion, apply the weights, and rank the results. Items that fit the budget and score high get accepted. Valuable items that do not fit get deferred, with a note on when they would be reconsidered. Items that score low and that nothing accepted depends on get rejected, with the reason recorded. Before finalising, I would trace dependencies so no accepted requirement is missing a prerequisite. The limitation is that the ratings involve judgement, and two people may rate differently, so I would recheck close calls with the stakeholders rather than trust a small gap in scores.
rubricPoints: Agrees explicit decision criteria and weights with stakeholders before scoring anything.
Rates each option against the criteria and ranks them, showing the reasoning.
Maps results to accept, defer, or reject, with a recorded reason for each decision.
Checks dependencies before rejecting or deferring a requirement.
Names a limit, such as subjective ratings or sensitivity of the ranking to the chosen weights.

suggested.rationale: A cost model that compares options in fictional credits would let the learner practise valuation and trade-offs on a planned engine, since no listed mission covers requirement decisions.

lessons.plain: Imagine a team with a long wish list and only so much time, money and people. Allocating requirements means sorting that list into what will be built now (accepted), what will wait for a later release (deferred), and what is dropped (rejected), while checking each choice against the limits on scope, schedule, budget and staff. The agreed result is a requirements baseline: a frozen version of the requirements that everyone builds and tests against. Without it, the project keeps changing shape and nobody can say whether it is on track.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has 40 requested features, room for about 25 in the next three months, and two engineers who are already fully booked. Before any teaching, what would you do first, and what would you need to know before deciding which features get in?
lessons.teach:
A requirements baseline is the agreed, approved set of requirements that the project will build and test against. It changes only through a formal change request, often called change control. Allocating requirements means deciding, for each candidate requirement, whether it is accepted (committed to the baseline), deferred (kept for a later release) or rejected (dropped). Each decision is checked against constraints. Scope is what the release includes, schedule is the time window, budget is the money or credits available, and resources are the people with the skills needed. A constraint is a limit you cannot quietly exceed. This works because a requirement that does not fit shows up on paper, where changing it is cheap, instead of halfway through the build.

Worked example. Candidates: R1 driver check-in (must, 5 days, needs a mobile developer); R2 PDF export (should, 3 days, mobile developer); R3 dark mode (could, 4 days); R4 single sign-on (must, 8 days, needs a security engineer who is free only from week 6); R5 map filter (should, 2 days). Capacity: 12 working days before release, one mobile developer, and the security engineer unavailable until week 6. Step 1: the two musts total 13 days, one over capacity, so the team must raise this with the sponsor rather than silently dropping one. Step 2: accept R1, running total 5. Step 3: accept R2, total 8. Step 4: accept R5, total 10. Step 5: defer R3, and defer R4 to the next release with sponsor agreement, because its engineer is not free until week 6. The baseline holds R1, R2 and R5 at 10 of 12 days, and each deferral has a recorded reason.

Common mistake: sorting by whoever asked loudest, or adding up estimates without checking who each item needs. Consequence: a must-have is discovered unstaffed mid-release, test plans collapse, and the baseline has to be reopened under change control. A baseline is credible only when every accepted item fits all four constraints at once.

questions.prompt: A regional food bank is planning a volunteer-shift app. The release window is 3 weeks, which gives 15 working days of capacity, with one back-end developer and a data privacy reviewer who is free only from week 4. The candidates are: S1 volunteer sign-up (priority must, 6 days, needs the back-end developer); S2 printable rota (priority should, 4 days, needs the back-end developer); S3 SMS reminders (priority could, 3 days); S4 consent recording (priority must, 5 days, needs the privacy reviewer). Work through the allocation. Step 1: the two musts total 11 days, which fits within 15, so there is no day-count problem to escalate. Step 2: accept S1, running total 6. Step 3: accept S2, running total 10. Step 4: [missing]. Which step completes the allocation correctly?
choices: Accept S4 anyway because it is labelled must, and musts are always in the baseline no matter who is available.
Reject S4 permanently, because a must that cannot be staffed in this window should be removed from the project altogether.
Accept S4 and S3 together, since the 5 spare days cover both and the privacy reviewer can join during week 3 unpaid.
Defer S4 with a recorded reason and sponsor agreement, because the privacy reviewer is not free until after the release window closes, and then stop because the other items fit.
questions.why: S4 fails the resource constraint because the only person who can do it is unavailable inside the window, so it is deferred with a recorded reason rather than accepted or rejected outright.

questions.prompt: A bike-share company's project lead is asked which statement about a requirements baseline is correct.
choices: It is a running wish list that the team edits whenever a stakeholder sends a new idea by email, so that nothing requested is ever lost during the project.
It holds every candidate requirement it was ever considered for, including the ones that were rejected, so that the history of decisions is kept in one place.
It is the agreed, approved set of requirements that the project builds and tests against, and it changes only through a formal change request.
It is written once at the start of the project, set aside, and never revisited, even after a budget or staffing constraint changes during the build.
questions.why: A baseline is defined as the approved set that changes only through formal change control, which is the only option that states this correctly.

questions.prompt: A clinic's appointment-reminder project has a 4-week release with 8 working days of capacity and one front-end developer. A candidate must-have (priority must, 3 days) needs an accessibility tester who is free only from week 5. What is the right way to allocate this candidate?
choices: Defer it with a recorded reason and sponsor agreement, because the tester is not available inside the window and the resource constraint cannot be quietly exceeded.
Reject it, because a candidate that cannot start in the first four weeks has no value to the release and should be dropped from the project.
Accept it, because must-have items are never removed from the baseline and the tester can be asked to start early or work extra hours if needed.
Accept it at the top of the list and then remove the lowest-priority item that is already accepted to make room for the tester's schedule.
questions.why: Because the tester is unavailable inside the release window, the item fails a constraint and must be deferred with a recorded reason, not silently accepted or dropped.

questions.prompt: A logistics team has 20 working days of capacity before its release. It accepts four items totalling 18 days, which fits the day count. Two of the items need the same database specialist, who has only 6 days free in that window, while those two items together need 9 days. Which conclusion is correct?
choices: The baseline is credible, because the total of 18 days is below the 20 days of capacity, so the four accepted items fit.
Both items can stay accepted, because a specialist who is short of time can usually work extra hours to close the gap without limit.
The baseline is not credible yet, because the specialist constraint is broken even though the total days fit, so one item must be deferred or the resourcing changed.
Only scope needs checking at this stage, and the specialist shortage can be sorted out during the build without changing the baseline.
questions.why: A baseline is credible only when every accepted item fits all the constraints at once, and here the specialist limit is exceeded even though the overall day count looks fine.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would turn a long list of requests into a requirements baseline that respects our scope, schedule, budget and staffing limits. Name one limit or tradeoff that makes the result less than ideal.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing every candidate requirement with its priority, its effort estimate and the specific skills it needs. Then I would lay those against the hard limits: how many working days remain before release, what budget applies, and who is actually available and when. I would commit the must-haves first and add should-haves while the running total stays within capacity, checking that each item's skill need is covered by someone free in the right week. Anything that does not fit is deferred or rejected with a recorded reason. The main tradeoff is that the baseline is only as good as the estimates. If they are rough, I would keep a small buffer, treat the baseline as frozen only after sponsor sign-off, and send later changes through change control.
rubricPoints: Defines a requirements baseline as an approved set that changes only through formal change control
Distinguishes accepted, deferred and rejected requirements, with a stated reason for each
Checks total effort against scope, schedule and budget, and against the availability of specific people
Escalates a must-have that cannot fit instead of dropping it silently

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a constrained allocation case adds the most here, and no listed mission or planned engine yet covers scope and staffing trade-offs directly.

lessons.plain: Once a group has agreed on what a solution must do, someone has to make that agreement official. Sign-off means the people with authority to approve the list say yes to it, and the approved list becomes the baseline, the fixed reference point that later changes are measured against. Getting there is rarely one person saying yes. People disagree about priorities, so the business analyst uses decision methods, structured ways of turning a pile of opinions into a clear group choice, to move the group toward agreement. The goal is that nobody is surprised later by a requirement they never accepted.
lessons.guessPrompt: A group of five stakeholders reviews a list of 40 requirements. Three want to approve it today and two want to hold off. What would you do before asking anyone for a signature, and why?
lessons.teach:
A requirements baseline is the agreed, versioned set of requirements that the project will work from. Sign-off is the recorded approval of that set by the people who hold decision authority, meaning those with the right to accept scope and to change it. A decision-making technique is a defined rule for turning several people's views into one outcome. Common rules include unanimity (everyone must agree), majority (more than half must agree), plurality (the largest group wins, even without a majority), and autocratic decision (one named person decides after hearing input). Multi-criteria scoring is another technique: each option is rated against weighted criteria such as value, risk and cost, so the group compares options on the same scale. Consensus means the group reaches agreement that every member can live with, even if not everyone's first choice.

The reason these techniques work is that a baseline only holds if the people who can change scope have accepted it. Agreeing the decision rule before the vote stops people from changing the rules when they dislike the result.

Worked example. Six requirements are up for sign-off with five stakeholders. Step 1: confirm the sponsor and two business owners are the named approvers. Step 2: agree in advance that a simple majority of named approvers decides. Step 3: present each requirement with its rationale and dependencies. Step 4: vote. Requirements 1 to 4 get four yes votes each. Requirement 5 gets two yes and three no; discussion shows it conflicts with a budget constraint, so the group defers it to the next release. Step 5: record the approvers, the date, the approved items and the deferred items as the baseline version.

Common mistake: treating silence or a lukewarm nod as agreement, or recording a verbal yes without writing down exactly what was approved. A running delivery then builds a requirement nobody truly accepted, it is rejected at acceptance testing, and the dispute restarts.

Changes that arrive after sign-off go through change control against the recorded version, so the baseline stays a reliable reference.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm has three named approvers: the operations director, the finance lead and the warehouse manager. Before the vote they agree that a simple majority of the named approvers decides. Step 1: confirm the three approvers. Step 2: agree the majority rule. Step 3: present five requirements, each with its rationale and dependencies. Step 4: vote. Requirement A gets three yes votes. Requirement B gets two yes and one no. Requirement C gets three yes. Requirement D gets one yes and two no. Requirement E gets three yes. Step 5 is missing. Which action completes the process?
choices: Hold a second vote on requirement D repeatedly until it finally passes with unanimous support from all three approvers
Record the approvers, the date, the approved items A, B, C and E, and deferred item D as the baseline version
Send all five requirements to change control before anything is recorded as approved
Accept requirement D because the warehouse manager spoke in its favour during discussion
questions.why: Step 5 is recording the approvers, date, approved items and deferred items as the baseline version, which is the exact written record the process requires once the decision rule has produced its outcome.

questions.prompt: A team has eight named approvers. The agreed rule is a simple majority of named approvers. A requirement receives four yes votes, three no votes and one abstention. What is the outcome under the agreed rule?
choices: Approved, because abstentions are not counted at all
Not approved, because the rule required unanimous agreement
Not approved, because four is not more than half of eight named approvers
Approved, because the yes votes outnumber the no votes
questions.why: A simple majority of eight named approvers requires more than half, so five yes votes are needed, and four yes votes fall short.

questions.prompt: During a review meeting, a business owner says 'that's fine by me' about a set of requirements, but nobody writes down which items were approved or who approved them. The team later treats this as the signed-off baseline. What is the main problem?
choices: Consensus cannot be reached in a meeting, so no decision can ever be recorded
A verbal, unrecorded nod does not show exactly what was approved or by whom, so the baseline cannot be relied on as a reference
The business owner should have spoken after the sponsor, not before
The team should have used plurality instead of majority
questions.why: A baseline is only useful if the approvers and the approved items are recorded precisely, and an unrecorded verbal response leaves that unclear, which is how disputes restart later.

questions.prompt: Three options are scored on weighted criteria using a 1 to 5 scale: value has weight 3, risk has weight 2, and cost has weight 1. Option X scores value 4, risk 3, cost 5. Option Y scores value 5, risk 2, cost 3. Option Z scores value 3, risk 5, cost 3. Which option has the highest weighted total?
choices: Option Y, because it scores highest on value
Option X, with a weighted total of 23
Option X and Option Z are tied at 23
Option Z, because it scores highest on risk, at 22
questions.why: Option X totals 12 plus 6 plus 5, which is 23, while Option Y totals 22 and Option Z totals 22, so X has the highest weighted total.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose a decision-making technique to obtain sign-off on the requirements baseline, and name one limit or tradeoff of the technique you pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by confirming who has decision authority, because a vote among people without authority does not produce a valid sign-off. Then I would choose the technique based on the situation. If the stakeholders are aligned and the cost of disagreement is high, I would aim for consensus through a structured review. If we are short on time and the approvers are clear, I would use a majority vote of named approvers, agreed before the vote. For competing options I would use multi-criteria scoring so the trade-offs are visible. Whichever method I pick, I would record the outcome, the approvers and the deferred items. The main tradeoff of majority voting is that the losing minority may feel overruled and push back later, so I would keep their concerns recorded and visible for change control.
rubricPoints: Confirms who holds decision authority before any vote
Matches the technique (consensus, majority, scoring, autocratic) to the situation
Agrees the decision rule before the vote
Names a real limit or tradeoff of the chosen technique
Records approvers, decision and deferred items as the baseline

suggested.rationale: Choosing and justifying a decision technique for a specific situation is best practised by explaining it back, and no listed mission or planned engine covers this objective.

lessons.plain: A requirements specification is the written description of what a system must do, written clearly enough that a builder and a tester can work from it without guessing. Imagine ordering a bridge by saying 'make it strong and pretty'. Nobody could check that. A good specification replaces vague wishes with statements that name who needs what, under which conditions, and how you would know it is done. You can write these as a short story from a user's point of view, as a step-by-step scenario of an interaction, or as a list of the data and connection details a system exchanges with others. The style varies, but the test of quality stays the same: could someone build it and prove it works?
lessons.guessPrompt: A team writes the requirement 'The app should load quickly.' Before any teaching, what is wrong with this sentence, and what single change would make it something a developer could build and a tester could check?
lessons.teach:
A requirements specification is the written statement of what a solution must do, detailed enough that developers can build it and testers can check it. Three common forms appear in this objective. A user story is a short sentence in the form 'As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]', describing one small piece of value. A use case describes an interaction step by step. It names an actor (anyone or anything outside the system that starts the interaction), a goal, preconditions (what must be true before it begins), a main flow of steps, and alternative or error flows. Data and interface details name the fields, formats, units, and the connections between systems that a feature depends on.

Why this works: a statement is actionable only when a builder can act on it without asking follow-up questions, and measurable only when someone can observe a pass or fail. Each requirement should therefore carry a condition and an observable result. Take the vague line 'Dispatchers should see vehicle positions quickly.' Name the actor: a dispatcher. Name the condition: a vehicle reports a new position. Add the measure: the position appears on the dispatcher's map within 5 seconds of receipt, for 95 percent of reports during peak load. Name the data: latitude and longitude as numbers, and a timestamp in one fixed time zone. Now a tester can run a test, and a developer knows the target.

The common mistake is writing the solution instead of the need, such as 'Use a particular cache product for positions'. This hides the real requirement and locks in a design before anyone has checked it against the goal. Keep the need, and let the design be chosen later.

In a running system, a requirement without a measure such as 'quickly' can produce a build that passes review but fails at peak traffic, and the argument afterwards becomes about interpretation rather than fact. A specification that states the measure lets the team find that failure before release.

questions.prompt: A regional food bank runs a volunteer scheduling system. A product owner wrote: 'Volunteers should see open shifts easily.' The analyst has filled in these parts: the actor is a registered volunteer; the condition is that a coordinator creates or releases a shift; the data is shift date as a calendar date, start time in 24-hour format, and a location code. The measure is still missing. Which completion makes the requirement measurable and actionable?
choices: Open shifts display on the volunteer's screen whenever the system is convenient for most users.
The system uses a Redis cache for open-shift data so that reads stay fast under load.
Volunteers can see open shifts through a list view that uses the food bank's standard colour scheme.
A newly released shift appears on the volunteer's open-shift list within 10 seconds of release, for 95 percent of releases during the Saturday morning peak.
questions.why: Only the third choice adds an observable pass or fail threshold, tied to the stated condition and to peak load, without dictating a design.

questions.prompt: Which statement is written in the user story form described in the teaching text?
choices: Receptionists need appointment slots shown quickly, with a timestamp in UTC.
The appointment page uses a grid layout with three columns and a search box at the top.
The scheduling tool must store shift times in a relational table with a foreign key to locations.
As a clinic receptionist, I want to see the next free appointment slot, so that I can book patients without calling the scheduler.
questions.why: A user story follows the pattern 'As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]', and only the second choice has all three parts in that order.

questions.prompt: A team's requirement says the parking permit portal should process renewals fast. What is the most direct consequence of leaving this unmeasured?
choices: The portal will lose its actor and no longer have a defined goal.
The build can pass review yet fail under peak renewal traffic, and the team will argue about what fast meant instead of checking a fact.
The tester will write too many use cases for the renewal flow.
Developers will be forced to use a specific payment vendor.
questions.why: Without a stated measure, a build can look acceptable in review but fail at peak load, and the dispute then turns on interpretation rather than observable evidence.

questions.prompt: In a use case for a clinic's patient check-in kiosk, which element states what must be true before the interaction begins?
choices: The precondition, such as the patient already having a booked appointment in the system.
The main flow, which lists the numbered steps from patient greeting to printing the slip.
The alternative flow, which covers the patient typing a wrong date of birth.
The actor, which is the receptionist who staffs the front desk.
questions.why: Preconditions are the conditions that must hold before the use case starts, whereas the main flow, alternative flow, and actor are different elements of the use case.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who will write test cases why a requirement such as 'the report should be accurate' must be rewritten. Then name one limit or tradeoff of the user story form compared with a use case.
lessons.modelAnswer: 'Accurate' cannot be tested because two people can disagree about what it means, so I would ask what the report must match and to what tolerance. For example, totals must equal the source file to the cent, and rows with missing fields must be listed rather than silently dropped. The tradeoff with user stories is that they are short and conversational, so they capture the reason for a feature well but leave out the error paths, data formats, and step order that a developer and tester need. A use case covers those details but takes longer to write and can feel heavy for a small change. In practice I would use a story to name the value, use a use case or data table to pin down the edge cases, and attach measurable acceptance criteria to both so we can tell when the work is done.
rubricPoints: Flags vague words such as accurate or fast as untestable.
Rewrites the requirement with an actor, a condition, and a measurable or observable result.
Names the data, format, or interface detail the builder needs.
States a tradeoff: user stories are brief but miss error paths, while use cases are complete but heavier.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine has learners write requirement specifications, so reading the worked forms is the best fit here.

lessons.plain: Validating requirements means checking, before anyone builds anything, that the written requirements are complete and actually serve the goal the business cares about. You do this three main ways: reading the documents against a checklist, showing a rough mock-up of the screens or behavior (a prototype) and asking people to react, and watching a working piece of the solution (a demo) and comparing it with what was asked. It checks the requirements themselves, not the finished product. Think of it like walking the owner through a building plan before construction starts, so mistakes are cheap to fix.
lessons.guessPrompt: A sponsor says the new order-tracking feature is ready to build because the requirements document was signed last month. Before anyone reviews it again, what questions would you ask to find out whether those requirements are really ready to build from?
lessons.teach:
Requirements validation is the check that a set of requirements is complete and aligned with the goals it is meant to serve. Completeness means every needed requirement is present and nothing obvious is missing. Alignment means each requirement traces back to a business goal, so nothing is built that nobody needs. Three techniques are common. A documentation review reads the written artifacts against a checklist, looking for gaps, contradictions, and vague words such as 'fast' or 'easy' that cannot be tested. A prototype is a rough model of screens or flow, kept low-fidelity so people feel free to criticise it; it tests whether people understand the requirement the way the writer meant. A demo shows a built or partly built capability live, and the reviewer checks it against the stated requirements.

Why it works: people spot mistakes far more readily when they see something than when they read abstract text, and a gap found on paper costs almost nothing to fix.

Worked example. The requirement reads: Dispatchers can see the vehicle's location. Step 1, documentation review: 'see' is undefined and freshness is not stated, so the requirement is flagged as not testable. Step 2, prototype: a map mock-up is shown to dispatchers, who say they also need the time of the last position update, otherwise they cannot tell whether the dot is stale. A missing requirement is found and added. Step 3, alignment: the stated goal is fewer missed pickups, and the requirement links to it, so it stays. Step 4, demo: once built, the team shows the map with a deliberately old timestamp to confirm the display matches the amended wording.

Common mistake: treating sign-off as validation. A signature shows agreement with the text, not that the text is complete or serves the goal.

In a running system the consequence is concrete: a map that is technically correct but silently shows old positions leads dispatchers to keep phoning drivers, and fixing it after release means rework across code, testing, and operations.

questions.prompt: A parts distributor's warehouse team has this requirement: Floor staff can record a stock count accurately. A stock write-off is stock removed from the books because it is lost or damaged. Step 1, documentation review: 'accurately' has no stated tolerance, so the requirement is flagged as not testable. Step 2, prototype: a paper-style count sheet mock-up is shown to three floor staff, who say they also need the bin location on every line, otherwise a recount cannot be checked, so a missing requirement is added. Step 4, demo: once built, the team enters a deliberately wrong count to confirm the system flags it against the amended wording. Step 3 is missing from the write-up. What should that step establish before the requirement counts as validated?
choices: That the warehouse manager has signed the requirement document, since a signature confirms the team agreed to it
That the count sheet prototype is detailed enough to print and hand out to staff on the floor
That the system can process ten thousand count lines a minute without slowing down
That each requirement, including the new bin location field, links to a stated business goal such as cutting stock write-offs, and any requirement with no such link is removed
questions.why: The missing step is the alignment check, which traces each requirement back to a business goal so nothing is kept that nobody needs, while the other choices describe sign-off, prototype fidelity, or performance, none of which tests alignment.

questions.prompt: A pharmacy chain writes this requirement: Refill reminders are sent promptly. In a documentation review, which finding best shows the requirement is not yet testable?
choices: The requirement does not name which of the chain's branches sends the reminders, so the server it runs on cannot be chosen
'Promptly' has no stated time limit, so no test can show whether a reminder passed or failed
The word 'reminders' is a noun, which makes the sentence grammatically incomplete for a formal document
The requirement is only one sentence long, so it must be missing a companion requirement somewhere else in the set
questions.why: A documentation review looks for vague words like 'promptly' that cannot be tested, and this one has no time limit a test could check against.

questions.prompt: A call centre's callback feature passes every stated requirement in a demo, yet customers still wait too long on the phone. Which validation gap most likely explains this?
choices: The tester wrote the requirements in the passive voice, which hides who is responsible for each action and so weakens the document
The demo used too few test calls to be statistically meaningful, so the result cannot be trusted for any conclusion at all
The demo was run on a laptop in a test room rather than on the production system, which changes only where the test happened and nothing about the requirements
Alignment to the wait-time goal was never checked, so a requirement that does not serve that goal could pass the demo unchallenged
questions.why: A demo checks the built feature against the stated requirements, so it cannot reveal a requirement that was never tied back to the goal of reducing wait time.

questions.prompt: In a prototype session, ten claims clerks review a rough screen flow for a new insurance claim tool. Five of them say they need a second approval field that is not in the written requirements. What does this finding indicate, and what should happen next?
choices: Treat it as a completeness gap: record the approval field as a requirement, then check that it traces to a business goal before keeping it
Sign off the original requirements now and raise the approval field as a change request after release, when it is cheaper to add
Replace the prototype with a demo, because demos always reveal missing requirements better than prototypes do
Ignore it, because feedback from clerks on a prototype is not a valid source of requirements
questions.why: Several users independently needing a field not in the text is evidence of a completeness gap, and the right response is to add it and then confirm it serves a goal, not to skip validation or defer it.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says that because the requirements were reviewed and signed off, we do not need to validate them again with a prototype or demo. Explain to them how validation differs from sign-off, and name one limit or tradeoff of using a prototype.
lessons.modelAnswer: Sign-off records that stakeholders agreed to the written text at a point in time. Validation checks something different: whether that text is complete, testable, and actually serves the goal it was meant to achieve. People can agree to a requirement and still have it be vague or missing a needed piece, and they often only notice when they see a concrete picture. A prototype makes that visible by showing screens or a flow that the reviewers can react to. The main limit is that a prototype is a simplified model. It can show the layout and steps but not real performance, real data volumes, or edge cases, so it can make people feel more certain than the evidence supports. That is why a demo of working behaviour is still needed later, and why each reviewed requirement should still be checked against its original goal rather than just the picture.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes sign-off (agreement to text) from validation (completeness and alignment checks)
Explains that a prototype reveals gaps and misunderstandings that reading alone misses
Names a concrete limit of prototypes, such as not showing performance, data scale, or edge cases
Notes that validation should trace each requirement back to a business goal

suggested.rationale: Choosing which validation technique fits a given situation is best practised by reasoning through an exam-style scenario, and no listed mission or planned engine covers requirements validation directly.

lessons.plain: When a project agrees to build something, people often write down what it should do, but a sentence like 'it should be fast' cannot be checked. This objective is about making those promises testable. A metric is a number you measure, such as how long a page takes to load. An acceptance criterion is a clear condition the finished solution must meet before the stakeholder agrees the requirement is done. Think of a home inspector who does not just say the house looks fine but checks specific measurements against an agreed standard. The better the measure and the threshold, the less room there is for argument at the end.
lessons.guessPrompt: A requirement says the new dispatch map should be 'fast.' Before reading on, what would you need to write down so that a tester could say clearly pass or fail?
lessons.teach:
A metric is a measurable quantity tied to a requirement, such as response time, error rate, or the share of records that match a source. A target is the value the metric must reach, and a measurement method says how and where it is collected. An acceptance criterion is a testable condition a solution must satisfy before a requirement is accepted. It combines a metric, a threshold, a condition of use, and a way to observe the result. Elaborating means adding these details until two independent testers reach the same pass or fail verdict.

Why it works: stakeholders and developers can only agree on what is measurable. Writing the criterion before build gives the design a fixed target and lets the team weigh trade-offs early, instead of arguing after delivery.

Worked example. Requirement: dispatchers need to see vehicle positions quickly. Step 1: choose a metric, the time from a vehicle reporting its position to that position appearing on the dispatcher's map. Step 2: set a threshold, 95 percent of updates within 5 seconds. Step 3: set the condition, normal operation with 400 active vehicles and peak operation with 800. Step 4: define the measurement, timestamps captured in the dispatcher's browser over seven days. Step 5: state the pass rule, which is that the criterion passes only if both load levels meet the threshold. Now a tester can say pass or fail without asking anyone.

Common mistake: measuring at the server only, which hides network and browser delay. The server may report one second while the dispatcher waits twenty seconds, so the criterion is accepted even though the user experience fails.

Consequence in a running system: dispatchers make decisions on positions that may be stale, so a criterion that does not measure what the user actually sees lets a slow system ship.

Acceptance criteria are only as good as the place they are measured from.

questions.prompt: A credit union wants its mobile app sign-in to feel quick. The team has drafted this acceptance criterion. The metric is the time from the member tapping Sign in to the account summary screen appearing. The threshold is 90 percent of sign-ins completing within 3 seconds. The condition of use is normal operation with 2,000 members signed in at once. The pass rule is that the criterion passes only if the threshold is met on both the Android and iPhone test devices. One step is still missing: where and how the timing is collected. Which completion makes the criterion testable?
choices: Ask the mobile app team to report their own timing figures after each release is built.
Measure the time until the first network packet leaves the phone and treat that moment as the finish point.
Record timestamps on the test phones from the tap to the summary screen appearing, across a two-week test period.
Read the server log entries for sign-in requests and report the average response time for the period.
questions.why: The measurement method must capture the same start and end points the member experiences, on the device the member uses, so the timestamps on the test phones match what a tester would see.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the four parts that make up an acceptance criterion, as described in the teaching text?
choices: The project's annual budget for the team that built the solution
A condition of use, such as the number of users active at once
A metric, such as response time or error rate
A way to observe the result, such as collected timestamps
questions.why: The four parts are a metric, a threshold, a condition of use, and a way to observe the result; the project budget is not part of a criterion.

questions.prompt: A claims processing system is measured by its vendor's server dashboard, which reports an average of 2 seconds per claim. Claims clerks say each claim takes about 15 seconds to appear on their screen. What is the most accurate fix to the acceptance criterion?
choices: Add a second server dashboard in a different data centre to confirm the 2-second average.
Lower the threshold from 2 seconds to 1 second so the server figure looks better.
Keep the server dashboard as the source, since the vendor's tool is the standard reference.
Measure from the clerk's screen, so the criterion captures the delay the user actually waits through.
questions.why: A criterion only reflects the user's experience if it is measured from where the user observes the result, not from a point upstream where delay is hidden.

questions.prompt: A draft criterion for a school timetable app reads: the schedule page should load fast. Two testers reading it would likely disagree on what counts as a pass. Which revision best allows both testers to reach the same verdict?
choices: The schedule page should feel responsive to most students during the school day.
Ninety-five percent of schedule page loads should finish within 3 seconds, measured by browser timestamps on a tablet over one school week, at 500 concurrent students.
The schedule page should load faster than the previous timetable app did last year.
The schedule page should load in under 3 seconds on a standard school Wi-Fi network.
questions.why: It states a metric, a threshold, a condition of use, and a measurement method, leaving no room for a subjective judgment of fast or responsive.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has only written vague requirements how you would turn one into measurable acceptance criteria, and name one limit or trade-off of the metric you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking what the user actually experiences, then pick one metric that captures it, such as the time from data being produced to it appearing on screen. Next I would set a threshold that stakeholders agree to, like 95 percent within five seconds, and state the conditions, such as normal and peak load. I would also write down where and how it is measured, because measuring at the server can hide delay the user feels. The trade-off is that a percentile target is easier to hit than a maximum, so the worst cases can still be bad. That is why I would also add a rule for how the criterion is judged, such as passing only when both load levels meet the threshold over a set window.
rubricPoints: Defines a metric as a measurable quantity and a criterion as a testable pass or fail condition
Explains that a threshold, condition of use, and measurement method are all needed
Notes that measurement location matters, since server-side numbers can hide user-visible delay
Names a real limit or trade-off, such as percentile targets allowing poor outliers
Shows that the criterion must allow two testers to reach the same verdict

suggested.rationale: No listed OpsForge mission or planned engine covers writing measurable acceptance criteria, so explaining the idea back to a teammate is the core skill to practise here.

lessons.plain: Tracing a requirement means keeping a clear chain of links from what stakeholders asked for to the work that was built and tested to meet it. Think of a delivery receipt that shows each item ordered, the box it was packed in, and the signature confirming it arrived. In a project, those links live in a traceability record, often a table or a tool, so anyone can later ask whether a promise was kept and point to proof. The goal is evidence: not 'we think it is done' but 'here is the test result and the release where it was shown to the sponsor.'
lessons.guessPrompt: Three months after go-live, a stakeholder asks whether the requirement that drivers see a vehicle's position within 10 seconds was actually delivered. What would you need on file to answer with proof rather than memory?
lessons.teach:
A requirement is a statement of a need or condition the solution must meet. A traceability link is a recorded connection between two items, such as a requirement and the test case that checks it. A traceability matrix is the table or tool view that holds these links. Forward traceability runs from a requirement to the design, build and tests that realize it; backward traceability runs from a built item or test back to the requirement that justifies it. A baseline is the agreed, approved version of the requirements at a point in time; changes after it go through change control. Evidence means an inspectable artifact showing the requirement was met, such as a passed test run, a recorded demo, or a signed acceptance.

Why it works: a requirement is only shown to be delivered if the link chain holds at the end. Links recorded as work happens are cheap; rebuilding them at go-live from memory is slow and error-prone.

Worked example. Requirement REQ-042: a dispatcher sees a vehicle's position updated within 10 seconds. Step 1: record the requirement with an ID, its source (the operations manager, interviewed on a known date) and its acceptance criterion, the 10-second limit. Step 2: link it forward to design element DE-7, the position-update service. Step 3: link it to test case TC-118, a load test that measures update latency. Step 4: when TC-118 runs and passes, attach that recorded result as evidence. Step 5: link the release, 3.2, where it shipped, and the sponsor demo record. The chain now runs from stakeholder need to inspectable proof.

Common mistake: marking a requirement done because its code was merged, with no linked test result. Merged code shows activity, not that the acceptance criterion was met.

Consequence: if the 10-second criterion changes later, the team can search the matrix and find DE-7, TC-118 and release 3.2 at once, instead of discovering the dependency in production. A traced requirement is delivered only when every link points to a result someone could inspect.

questions.prompt: A regional credit union's loan team tracks REQ-LN-31: a loan officer must see a submitted application's status within 5 seconds. Step 1: REQ-LN-31 is recorded with its ID, its source (the branch manager, interviewed on 12 May) and its 5-second acceptance criterion. Step 2: it is linked forward to design element DE-22, the status-query module. Step 3: it is linked to test case TC-340, a timing test that measures the delay from submission to the status being displayed. Step 4 is missing. TC-340 is then run and passes. Which action completes step 4 so the requirement can be treated as delivered?
choices: Delete the TC-340 link now that the test has passed, to keep the matrix short
Mark REQ-LN-31 as done because DE-22 was merged into the main code branch
Ask the branch manager to confirm verbally that the status screen looks right
Attach the recorded passing TC-340 run to REQ-LN-31 as evidence
questions.why: Evidence is the inspectable, passed test result tied to the requirement's criterion, while merged code or a verbal check does not show the 5-second limit was met.

questions.prompt: In a traceability context, what is a traceability matrix?
choices: The table or tool view that holds the recorded links between items such as requirements and tests
The sponsor's record of the planned release date for each feature
A running list of every defect found during testing, ordered by severity
The signed document that approves the requirements at one point in time
questions.why: The teaching text defines the matrix as the table or tool view that holds the traceability links, not as the approval document, defect log or schedule.

questions.prompt: A build item BLD-9, an export feature, appears in the repository but is linked to no requirement. A reviewer wants to find the requirement that justifies it. Which direction of traceability does this call for?
choices: A baseline comparison of the approved requirement versions against the current ones
Attaching a demo record to BLD-9 as evidence of delivery
Backward traceability, from the built item back to the requirement that justifies it
Forward traceability, from the requirement to the design, build and tests that realize it
questions.why: Backward traceability starts at a built item or test and runs back to the requirement that justifies it, which is what the reviewer needs for BLD-9.

questions.prompt: After the baseline was approved, the acceptance criterion for REQ-Q5 was tightened from 30 days to 14 days. The matrix shows REQ-Q5 linked to design element DE-4, test case TC-51 and release 2.0. What is the correct first response?
choices: Edit the criterion in the matrix directly and keep the old passing result for TC-51 as evidence
Leave the baseline as it is, since the tests already passed against the old limit
Route the change through change control, then use the linked DE-4, TC-51 and release 2.0 to judge what must be revised and retested
Close REQ-Q5 as delivered, because its code was merged before the change was requested
questions.why: Changes after the baseline go through change control, and the recorded links show which design, test and release items the changed criterion affects.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who says 'we merged the code, so it is traced' how you would show a stakeholder that a requirement was delivered. Name one limit of the traceability record and one tradeoff in how much detail to keep.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd tell them a requirement counts as delivered only when its chain of links runs from the stated need, through the design item and build, to a test case with a recorded passing result and the release where it shipped. Merged code only shows activity, not that the acceptance criterion was met. The main limit is that a matrix only proves what was linked; if a link was never recorded, the record can look complete while a gap hides. The tradeoff is detail: linking every line of code makes the matrix unmanageable, so I'd link at the level of requirements, design elements, tests and releases, keeping the depth a sponsor or auditor would actually ask about.
rubricPoints: Delivery is shown by a complete chain from the stated need to an inspectable test result and release, not by merged code alone
Evidence means a recorded artifact such as a passed test run or signed acceptance
A traceability record only proves what was actually linked, so gaps can hide
Detail must be balanced: link at a useful level, not every line of code

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practices requirement traceability, so an exam-style situation to reason through about which evidence proves delivery is the best fit.

lessons.plain: Monitoring requirements through their lifecycle means checking, at every stage a requirement passes through, that the supporting paperwork and checks it needs have actually been produced and looked over by someone other than the author. A requirement is a stated need, such as what a system must do. As it moves from first idea to approved, built and tested, it should be backed by things like diagrams, written descriptions and test cases. The business analyst keeps watch so that a requirement never advances on words alone. Think of a building inspector who signs off each floor before the next one goes up.
lessons.guessPrompt: A requirement is marked approved, but nobody can point to a written, measurable acceptance criterion for it. Should it be allowed to move on to build, and what would you check first?
lessons.teach:
A lifecycle is the ordered set of stages a requirement passes through, such as proposed, analysed, approved, built and verified. An artifact is any document or model that records or supports the requirement. Examples include a process model (a diagram of steps), a data definition (the fields and what each one means), a requirement statement with acceptance criteria (the conditions that prove it is met), and a test case (a scripted check with an expected result).
