Monitoring means confirming, at each stage, that the artifacts that stage calls for exist and have been reviewed, before the requirement is allowed to move on. Review means a second person checks the artifact against its source, such as the stakeholder's stated need, and records acceptance or the issues found.

This works because each stage builds on the one before. A test case written from a vague statement will only be as precise as that statement. If the gap is not caught at the approval gate, it surfaces at test time, when changing it is expensive.

Worked example. A dispatcher needs to see a vehicle's position updated within ten seconds. Step 1, analysed: the analyst produces a process model of how positions reach the dispatch screen and a data definition for the timestamp field, and a reviewer checks both against the dispatcher's interview notes. Step 2, approved: the requirement carries a measurable acceptance criterion (an update is visible within ten seconds for 95 percent of readings), and the stakeholder signs it. Step 3, verified: test cases are written from that criterion and traced back to it. The monitor confirms all three artifacts exist and were reviewed before the status moves forward.

Common mistake: treating monitoring as a status column. A requirement marked approved with no reviewed criterion looks tracked but is not monitored. Consequence: if the ten-second criterion is missing at approval, the build team guesses a threshold, testers check against a different one, and the dispute appears only after release. Monitoring means checking the evidence, not just the status label.

questions.prompt: A county library runs an overdue-notice feature. The requirement is that a patron receives a notice within 48 hours of a loan's due date. Stage 1, analysed: the analyst produces a process model of how overdue loans are found and notices are sent, and a data definition for the due-date field. A reviewer checks both against the librarian's interview notes and records acceptance. Stage 2, approved: the requirement is rewritten with a measurable criterion (a notice is queued within 48 hours of the due date for 99 percent of loans), and the librarian signs it. One step is still missing from Stage 2. Which step completes Stage 2 before the requirement may move to Stage 3?
choices: The build team picks a notice-queue threshold on its own if the criterion seems unclear.
The tester writes test cases from the criterion and traces them back to it.
A second person reviews the criterion against the librarian's stated need and records acceptance or the issues found.
The requirement's status column is changed to approved.
questions.why: Review means a second person checks an artifact against its source and records the result, and the criterion is a Stage 2 artifact that must be reviewed before the requirement advances.

questions.prompt: In this course, what does monitoring a requirement through its lifecycle mean?
choices: Writing every test case at the start so that later stages have nothing left to do.
At each stage, confirming that the artifacts that stage calls for exist and have been reviewed before the requirement moves on.
Counting how many change requests a requirement attracts over its life.
Updating the status column each time someone mentions the requirement in a meeting.
questions.why: The teaching text defines monitoring as checking, stage by stage, that the required artifacts exist and were reviewed before the requirement is allowed to advance, not just tracking a status label.

questions.prompt: A fleet fuel-card team has a requirement that the monthly fuel report must match card statements within 0.5 percent. The status shows approved, but no measurable criterion or review record exists for it. Six weeks later, testers check the report against a 2 percent tolerance that the build team had guessed. What is the root failure?
choices: The analyst should have produced more process models for the report.
The status label was treated as evidence, and the approval gate did not confirm that a reviewed criterion existed.
The testers were given too little time to run the checks.
The fuel card vendor changed its statement format partway through.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that a requirement marked approved without a reviewed criterion looks tracked but is not monitored, and that a guessed threshold causes disputes later.

questions.prompt: A warehouse picking app has a requirement that pick lists appear within 3 seconds for 90 percent of requests. The team is at the verification stage. Which evidence should the monitor confirm before allowing the requirement to be marked verified?
choices: Test cases built from the developer's code comments instead of the stated criterion.
A developer note saying the build looked fine in a quick manual run, with the status set to verified.
A new 5-second criterion written after testing so that the build passes.
Test cases written from the 3-second, 90 percent criterion and traced back to it, with their expected results reviewed.
questions.why: At the verification stage the monitor checks that test cases were written from the approved criterion, traced back to it, and reviewed, rather than accepting a status change or a loosened target.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what it means to monitor a requirement through its lifecycle, and name one limit or tradeoff of checking artifacts at every stage.
lessons.modelAnswer: Monitoring a requirement through its lifecycle means that at each stage I check the supporting artifacts the stage calls for exist and have been reviewed before the status moves on. For example, before a requirement is approved, I want a measurable acceptance criterion and a stakeholder's sign-off on it. Before it is verified, I want test cases traced back to that criterion. The main limit is cost. Reviews take time, and checking every artifact at every gate can slow a small project or create paperwork nobody reads. So I scale the depth of review to risk. A safety or billing requirement gets a full review at each gate, while a low-risk cosmetic change may need only a quick check that the criterion exists. The tradeoff is accepting some delay in exchange for not discovering gaps during testing or after release, when they are far more expensive to fix.
rubricPoints: Defines monitoring as checking that stage artifacts exist and have been reviewed before the status advances
Gives a concrete example of an artifact expected at a specific stage, such as acceptance criteria before approval
Names a limit or tradeoff, such as review cost or delay to the schedule
Explains that gaps caught late are more expensive to fix than gaps caught at the gate

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a stage-by-stage gate situation adds the most, and no listed mission or planned engine covers requirement lifecycle artifacts.

lessons.plain: A requirement is a stated need the project must meet, and it does not stay the same from the day it is written to the day it is delivered. It moves through stages such as proposed, approved, in design, built, tested and accepted. Updating its status means changing its recorded stage whenever something real happens, and communicating that status means telling the people who depend on it. Recording the change in the traceability tool, the shared log that links each requirement to its related work and evidence, keeps the record honest. A status that is out of date is worse than no status, because people act on it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A developer tells you a requirement is 'done' because the code is written, but nobody has tested it and the customer has not accepted it. What status would you record instead, and why would writing 'done' cause trouble later?
lessons.teach: A lifecycle state is a named stage a requirement occupies, such as Proposed, Approved, Implemented, Verified, Accepted, Deferred or Rejected. A status transition is a move from one state to the next. Each transition has an entry condition, meaning the evidence that must exist before the move is allowed. A traceability tool is the shared record, often a repository or spreadsheet, that links each requirement to its models, test cases, changes and approvals. Why it works: a status is a claim about the project, and the claim is only trustworthy when each state points to an artifact that proves it. Worked example, for a requirement REQ-42 that says dispatchers receive an alert within 5 seconds of a geofence breach. Step 1: when a stakeholder raises it, log it as Proposed and record the source. Step 2: when the sponsor approves it into the baseline, move it to Approved and record the approver and date. Step 3: when the build is finished, move it to Implemented and link the build. Step 4: when test case TC-108 passes, move it to Verified and record the test run. Step 5: when the dispatch supervisor signs off, move it to Accepted and record that sign-off. After each move, tell the project manager and affected stakeholders, because the release decision depends on it. Common mistake: marking a requirement done at Implemented, skipping Verified, or changing status verbally without a linked record. Consequence: the release report shows full delivery while the 5-second alert rule was never tested, and the first real breach in production goes unnoticed. A status change is only complete when the new state, its evidence and the people informed are all recorded together.

questions.prompt: A payroll company tracks REQ-17, which says employees can download a payslip as a PDF within 3 seconds of asking. Step 1: the HR lead raised it, and it was logged as Proposed with the HR lead named as source. Step 2: the CFO approved it into the baseline, so it was moved to Approved with the CFO and the date recorded. Step 3: the steering committee chose to push the requirement to release 4 to free up capacity, so it was moved to Deferred and the committee's decision was recorded as the evidence. The one missing piece is that nobody has told the HR lead or the payroll manager about the move. Which completion makes the status change complete?
choices: Move the requirement back to Proposed so the committee's decision is approved again first.
Retest the 3-second rule now so the Deferred move has a passing test run attached to it.
Inform the HR lead and payroll manager of the Deferred move and record that notice alongside the change.
The record is complete, since a Deferred requirement needs no message because no work is happening on it.
questions.why: A status change is only complete when the new state, its evidence and the people informed are all recorded together, so the missing notice must be sent and recorded.

questions.prompt: A freight company's requirement REQ-9 says customs declarations are auto-filled from the shipment record. The build is finished and the requirement has been moved to Implemented. Which evidence must exist before it can move to Verified?
choices: A stakeholder's email saying the feature looks good.
A list of every change request that touched the shipment module this quarter.
The original source note from the operations lead who raised it.
A passing test run linked to the requirement's test case.
questions.why: Verified is reached when a passing test run exists and is linked to the requirement, because that run is the entry condition that proves the requirement works.

questions.prompt: A team agreed in a meeting that REQ-31 is Accepted and changed its status verbally, with no linked record. What is the most direct consequence?
choices: The tool automatically reverts the requirement to Proposed.
Nothing, since meeting minutes count as a linked record.
The change stays hidden in the tool until the next baseline review is held.
The Accepted status points to no evidence, so the claim cannot be checked later.
questions.why: A status is a claim that is only trustworthy when it points to an artifact, so an Accepted status with no linked record cannot be verified by anyone later.

questions.prompt: A sponsor rejects REQ-54, a freight-tracking map layer, in a steering meeting. Which record update is complete?
choices: Move it to Rejected, record the sponsor, date and reason, and inform the affected stakeholders.
Move it to Deferred so the reason can be reviewed later.
Delete REQ-54 from the tool entirely so the backlog stays clean and nobody sees the requirement again.
Leave it at Proposed until the next meeting, then mark it Rejected.
questions.why: A rejection is a status transition that needs its evidence and approver recorded and the affected people informed, so the move is complete only when all three are captured together.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who will update requirement statuses why a requirement should move to Verified only when linked test evidence exists, and name one limit or tradeoff of recording status changes this strictly.
lessons.modelAnswer: Verified is a claim that a requirement behaves as stated, so the record must point to something that shows it, such as a passing test case and its run. Without that link, the status is someone's opinion, and the release report will overstate what is delivered. The tradeoff is effort and speed. Every transition needs a linked artifact and a notice to stakeholders, which adds work for the team and can slow down progress on small changes. Some items may also sit in a state a little longer than reality because the evidence is still being gathered. The team should accept that small lag in exchange for a record that others can rely on, and should agree in advance on which evidence each state requires so the rule is applied the same way by everyone.
rubricPoints: Verified requires linked test evidence, not just a finished build.
Each state change is recorded in the traceability tool with its evidence and date.
Stakeholders and the project manager are told when status changes.
Names a real tradeoff, such as effort, speed, or a temporarily lagging status.

suggested.rationale: Requirement lifecycles are valid and invalid state transitions, which the planned workflow state machine engine would let the learner practise directly.

lessons.plain: Communicating requirements status means telling the project manager and stakeholders where each requirement stands right now, and flagging anything that could derail it. Think of a business analyst as the person keeping the project's shared map of what the software must do. A status update is not just a list of what is finished. It names the issues (open questions or blockers), conflicts (two stakeholders wanting incompatible things), changes (requests to alter agreed requirements), risks (things that might go wrong later), and an overall picture of health. Good updates are specific, dated, and say which decision is needed and from whom.
lessons.guessPrompt: A stakeholder tells you a requirement is basically done, but two other stakeholders have never reviewed it. What would you put in your status update to the project manager about it, and why?
lessons.teach:
A requirement's status is its current state in the project, such as proposed, under review, approved, in build, or delivered. Communicating that status means giving the project manager (the person who owns schedule, budget and delivery) and stakeholders (anyone with an interest in the outcome) a short, accurate picture. The update should separate five kinds of information. An issue is an open problem that blocks or slows work, such as an unanswered question. A conflict is a clash where two stakeholders need incompatible things. A change is a proposed or approved alteration to a requirement already agreed. Approved changes are measured against the requirements baseline, which is the agreed version everyone checks against. A risk is an event that has not happened yet but could hurt the project if it does. Overall status is a one-line judgement of whether the work is on track, at risk, or off track, backed by the evidence behind it.

Why it works: the project manager can only make decisions about schedule and resources from what reaches them. Naming each item with an owner and the decision needed turns a vague worry into an action.

Worked example. Requirement REQ-14, 'customers can cancel a pickup up to two hours before', is in build. Testing shows Finance wants a four-hour window for refunds. Step 1: this is a conflict, not yet a change, because the baseline still says two hours. Step 2: record REQ-14 as in conflict, naming both positions and their holders. Step 3: state the decision needed from the sponsor and the date it is needed by. Step 4: mark overall status as at risk, because the build may need rework. Only after the sponsor decides does the item become a change request, which is then assessed for impact.

Common mistake: reporting 'all on track' while a requirement waits on an unanswered question, so the project manager schedules it as finished.

Consequence: if the two-hour rule ships while refunds still assume four hours, customers and support see refund errors after release, and the rework lands at the worst time.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team has a requirement REQ-31, 'stock counts sync to the ERP every night'. Its integration lead reports that the nightly feed provider has announced its API will be retired on 15 March. Nothing has broken yet, and no change has been raised. Step 1: this has not happened yet and could hurt the project, so it is a risk, not an issue or a change. Step 2: record the risk against REQ-31, naming the integration lead as owner and 15 March as the retirement date. Step 3 is missing. Step 4: mark overall status as at risk, backed by the retirement date and the lack of a replacement feed. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Raise a change request to alter REQ-31 and assess its impact on the schedule.
State the decision the project manager needs, such as funding a replacement feed or accepting manual counts, and the date it is needed by, ahead of 15 March.
Wait until the API is retired, then record the problem as an issue.
Log the item as an issue and mark REQ-31 as blocked today.
questions.why: A risk update must name the decision the project manager has to make and the date it is needed by, which here means before the retirement date, whereas the other choices either skip ahead to a change that has not been agreed, misclassify a risk as a blocking issue, or wait until it is too late.

questions.prompt: A tester finds that the acceptance criterion for a login requirement is unanswered: nobody has said whether account lockout applies after 3 or 5 failed attempts, and the build is waiting on that answer. Which category does this belong to?
choices: Change, because a requirement is being altered.
Issue, because it is an open problem that is slowing work.
Risk, because the lockout rule might hurt the project later.
Conflict, because two stakeholders need incompatible things.
questions.why: An unanswered question that slows work is an issue by definition, while the other categories describe a future event, a clash between stakeholders, or an alteration to an agreed requirement.

questions.prompt: A status report marks the whole project as on track, but requirement REQ-40 is waiting on an unanswered question from the security team, so it is still unfinished. What is the main problem with the report?
choices: REQ-40 should be logged as a risk, since nothing has happened yet.
Only approved changes belong in a status update, so REQ-40 should be left out entirely.
The report is fine, because overall status is a judgement and this is only one item.
Overall status is misleading; the open issue on REQ-40 should lower it to at risk.
questions.why: Reporting on track while a requirement waits on an open issue is the common mistake, because the project manager may schedule the requirement as finished when it is not.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks to change REQ-52 from 30-day record retention to 45 days, and the sponsor approves the change yesterday. Which entry should the status update show for REQ-52?
choices: Record it as an approved change measured against the baseline, which still shows 30 days.
Record it as a risk until the build confirms that 45 days works.
Record it as a conflict, because the stakeholder asked for the change.
Update the baseline to 45 days so that the status matches the new agreement.
questions.why: An approved change is shown against the requirements baseline, which remains the agreed version until it is formally changed, so the update should show the 30-day baseline alongside the approved 45-day change.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a new teammate how you would report the status of a requirement that is both in conflict and at risk, and name one limit of a status report that the project manager should know about.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would report the requirement as its own item with its current lifecycle state, then separate the conflict from everything else. The conflict is that two stakeholders want incompatible things, so it goes in as a conflict with each position and its holder named, not as a vague issue. I would state the decision needed, who makes it, and the date it is needed by. The risk is what happens if that decision slips: rework after build or a missed release, so I would describe its likelihood and impact in plain words. Overall status would be at risk, with the evidence behind that judgement. One limit to flag is that a status report is a snapshot, only as current as the last review. Anything stakeholders have not yet confirmed should be marked unconfirmed rather than done.
rubricPoints: Separates conflicts, issues, changes and risks instead of lumping them together
Names the people holding each position and the decision owner
States the decision needed and by when
Gives an overall status backed by evidence
Notes that a status report is a snapshot and unconfirmed items must be marked as such

suggested.rationale: Explaining status items and their limits back to a teammate is the core skill, and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: When a project already has an agreed list of what it must deliver, someone will eventually ask to change one item. Managing that request means answering three questions before anyone says yes: what else does this touch, what depends on it, and how risky is the change. The agreed list is the reference point, and the rules for approving changes are written down in advance. Think of a house renovation: before moving a wall, you check which pipes and wiring run behind it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A stakeholder asks to change one requirement that was already approved and built into the plan. Before deciding anything, what three things would you want to know, and why would each matter?
lessons.teach:
A requirements baseline is the set of requirements that has been formally approved at a given point in time. It is the reference against which every later change is measured. A change-control plan is the agreed set of rules for handling changes: who may submit a request, what the request must contain, who approves it, and how the approved result is recorded. A change request is the formal written proposal to alter something in the baseline. An impact assessment is the analysis of what that change would affect, including other requirements, designs, tests, schedule, and cost. A dependency is a requirement or artifact that relies on another one, directly or through a chain. Risk here means the chance that the change causes a bad outcome, multiplied by how bad that outcome would be.

Worked example. Requirement R-12 in the baseline says dispatchers see vehicle positions refreshed every 10 seconds. A stakeholder asks for 2 seconds. Step one: log a change request against R-12 as the change-control plan requires. Step two: trace forward from R-12 using the traceability links. It connects to an ingest design element, to test case TC-31 that checks the 10-second rate, and to requirement R-19, which assumes the same feed. Step three: note the dependencies. A faster refresh changes the ingest load and may break R-19's timing assumptions. Step four: rate the risk. The feed's rate limit is unknown, so the risk is high. Step five: package the findings with options and send them to the approving body. The baseline is not edited until the change is approved, and then the new version is recorded.

A common mistake is editing the baseline text directly because the change looks small, or assessing only the requirement itself and missing the downstream links. In a running system, an unassessed refresh-rate increase can overload the ingest pipeline during a traffic surge and delay the positions dispatchers rely on. A change is only safe to approve once its impact on dependent artifacts has been shown.

questions.prompt: A credit union's baseline requirement BR-7 says loan applications are automatically declined when the applicant's debt ratio is above 40 percent. Leadership asks to raise the limit to 45 percent. The analyst has already logged a change request under the change-control plan. She traced forward from BR-7 and found three linked items: test case TC-88, which checks the 40 percent limit; requirement BR-21, a monthly regulator report that counts automatic declines using the 40 percent rule; and an underwriting design element that reads the threshold. She has noted that the change alters the number of declines and would make the BR-21 report inconsistent with the new rule, so the dependencies are recorded. The one step not yet done is rating the risk of the change before the findings go to the approving body. What should she do to complete that step?
choices: Edit BR-7 to read 45 percent so that the risk is judged against the new wording.
Wait until the change is approved and then rate the risk from the updated baseline.
Multiply the chance that the change causes a bad outcome, such as a misstated regulator report, by how bad that outcome would be, and record the result with the findings.
Count the linked items and use that count as the risk score, since more links mean more risk.
questions.why: Risk in this framework is the chance of a bad outcome multiplied by its severity, so the analyst must weigh both factors and record the rating before approval.

questions.prompt: A coastal shipping firm's requirement set was formally approved on 3 March. Five weeks later a sponsor asks for a change to one requirement. Which document is the reference against which the impact of that change should be measured?
choices: The sponsor's most recent email describing the wanted change
The test results from last week's regression run
The requirements baseline as it was approved on 3 March
The draft requirements from the early design workshop
questions.why: The baseline is the formally approved set at a fixed point in time, and every later change is measured against it.

questions.prompt: A hotel booking system has requirement R-7, which sets guest check-in at 3 pm. A product manager wants it changed to 1 pm and plans to edit the wording of R-7 directly because the change looks small. Requirement R-30, which schedules room cleaning, assumes a 3 pm check-in. What should happen before the change is approved?
choices: Assess the impact on dependent items such as R-30 and its linked tests, then submit the change request for approval
Accept the change because it touches one requirement only
Confirm only that the wording of R-7 is grammatically correct
Edit R-7 now and fix R-30 later if anyone complains
questions.why: A change should be approved only after its impact on dependent artifacts has been shown, and editing the baseline text directly bypasses that step.

questions.prompt: A warehouse robot-routing requirement says the controller recalculates each robot's path every 5 seconds. A team proposes changing this to every 1 second. The controller's processing capacity is unknown, and a stalled path could cause a collision. Which statement correctly describes how to rate this change's risk?
choices: The risk is low because the change alters only one number in the requirement.
The risk is the chance of a bad outcome multiplied by how bad that outcome would be, so the unknown capacity and the collision severity both need to be weighed.
The risk equals the number of requirements that mention the controller.
The risk can be ignored until the controller vendor confirms the new rate.
questions.why: Risk combines likelihood and severity, and a small edit in the requirement text does not reduce either factor.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a new teammate how you would handle a requested change to an already approved requirement. Name one limit or tradeoff of the impact assessment you would run.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not change the approved requirement directly. First I would log a formal change request against it, following the change-control plan, so the request is recorded and goes to the right approver. Then I would trace forward from that requirement through its links to design elements, test cases, and any other requirements that depend on it. That shows the dependencies, and I would rate the risk of each affected item. I would package the findings as options with their cost and schedule effects and send them for a decision. The limit is that a trace only shows the links someone has recorded. If the traceability is incomplete, the assessment will miss real impacts, so I would say so in the package and state which areas I could not check.
rubricPoints: Changes go through the change-control plan as a formal request, not a direct edit to the baseline.
Impact is traced forward through recorded links to dependent requirements, designs, and tests.
Risk is assessed for each affected item, not only for the original requirement.
A limit is named, such as incomplete traceability or unknown external constraints.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style change scenario with a baseline and dependencies adds the most to this objective, and no listed mission or planned engine covers requirements change analysis.

lessons.plain: Validating test results means checking the proof that a finished solution works, measured against what the business actually asked for. It is not enough that tests passed or that a report looks tidy. You take each requirement and each acceptance criterion (the specific, testable conditions that say when a requirement counts as met) and ask three things: is there evidence that covers it, is that evidence current and trustworthy, and does it really show the condition was met? A passing test that checks the wrong thing is still a gap. The aim is to know, item by item, what is proven, what is not, and what has to happen next.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team reports that all 240 automated tests passed on a new order-tracking feature. The requirement says customers must see a delivery status update within 30 seconds of a change in the delivery system. What would you want to check before accepting that the requirement is met?
lessons.teach:
A requirement is a statement of what the solution must do for the business. An acceptance criterion is a testable condition attached to that requirement, such as a time limit, a value, or a result that must hold. Test evidence is the record that shows a test ran: its scope, the environment it ran in, the date, and the outcome. Traceability is the link from each requirement to the criteria and tests that cover it. Validation asks whether the evidence actually demonstrates each criterion, not whether a green build exists.

Tests only show what they were written to check, so the first question is always coverage. Worked example, using the 30-second rule. Step 1: write down the criterion exactly: a status change in the delivery system appears on the customer screen within 30 seconds. Step 2: find the test linked to it. Step 3: read what that test does. Suppose it writes a status directly into the database and checks the API returns it. That proves the API reads correctly, but not the full path from the delivery system to the screen, and not the timing. Step 4: check the evidence itself. Suppose the run used a test environment with a simulated two-second feed and was executed three weeks ago, before a change to the message queue. Step 5: record the result. The criterion is only partly evidenced, and the timing across the real path is unproven.

The common mistake is counting passed tests as proof, treating the number of tests as coverage. In a running system this matters because a release signed off on this evidence can reach customers showing status that is minutes old, and support tickets then reveal a gap nobody tested. Validation means tracing each criterion to evidence that really exercises it, and marking the ones that have none.

questions.prompt: A payroll system must email each payslip within 15 minutes of a pay run being approved. Step 1: the criterion is written exactly as stated. Step 2: the linked test is found. Step 3: the test is read. It calls the mail service directly with a fake employee record and confirms a send request was issued, without passing through the approval step or the scheduler. Step 4 is not shown here. Which action completes the check before the result is recorded?
choices: Count the passing payroll tests in the report to confirm the criterion is covered.
Check the test evidence's environment, run date, and whether the run included the approval-to-send path, since the criterion depends on that path.
Rewrite the criterion as payslips are emailed eventually so that it matches what the test proves.
Accept the result, because the mail service reported a successful send in the test.
questions.why: Step 4 is checking the evidence itself, meaning whether the environment, date, and path exercised match what the criterion depends on, so the correct choice is the one that examines those details.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what is an acceptance criterion?
choices: A testable condition attached to a requirement, such as a time limit, a value, or a result that must hold.
The link that connects each requirement to the tests that cover it.
A list of everyone who must approve a solution before release.
The written record of a test run showing its scope, environment, date, and outcome.
questions.why: The teaching text defines an acceptance criterion as a testable condition attached to a requirement, which matches the second choice; the other choices describe sign-off, test evidence, and traceability.

questions.prompt: A loyalty app has the criterion that a customer's points balance updates within 60 seconds of a purchase. The only linked test writes a balance straight into the ledger table and checks the balance screen shows it. The run used a stubbed payment feed and happened before the payment gateway was changed. What does validation conclude?
choices: The criterion is fully evidenced, because the balance screen showed the correct value in the test.
The criterion has no evidence at all, because the test used a stubbed payment feed.
The criterion is only partly evidenced, because the test does not exercise the real purchase-to-balance path or the 60-second timing.
The criterion is evidenced, because the gateway change does not affect balance display.
questions.why: The test checks only part of the path, uses a non-representative feed and an outdated run, so the timing across the real path is unproven, which makes the criterion only partly evidenced.

questions.prompt: A clinic booking system team reports 412 passing tests and proposes sign-off. What is the correct validation response?
choices: Accept sign-off, because a large number of passing tests shows broad coverage.
Approve the release only if every test was run in the production environment.
Ask the team to add more tests until the count passes 500, since more tests means more coverage.
Trace each acceptance criterion to a test that actually exercises it, and mark any criterion with no such test as unevidenced before deciding.
questions.why: Validation traces each criterion to evidence that really exercises it and marks gaps, because the number of passed tests is not coverage and a high count can hide untested criteria.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says, 'All the tests passed, so we can sign this off.' Explain to them, in your own words, what you would check in the test results, reports and evidence against the requirements and acceptance criteria before agreeing, and name one limit of this kind of validation that they should keep in mind.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not accept 'all passed' on its own. I would take each acceptance criterion and find the specific test linked to it, then read what that test actually does. I would check the evidence too: which environment it ran in, when, and whether it covers the real path or a shortcut. Any criterion with no linked evidence, or only evidence that skips part of the path, goes on the open list. The limit to remember is that a test only proves what it was designed to check, so a clean result can still miss conditions that nobody wrote a test for, such as timing under real load or behaviour in production data. Passing tests reduce risk, but they do not replace comparing the evidence against the requirements.
rubricPoints: Check each acceptance criterion against the specific test or evidence linked to it, not against overall pass counts
Examine the evidence itself: environment, date, scope and whether it covers the real path
Record criteria with no evidence or partial evidence as open gaps before sign-off
Name a limit: tests only prove what they were designed to check, so untested conditions can still fail

suggested.rationale: Judging whether evidence really covers a criterion is best learned by reasoning through an exam-style situation with mixed test results and gaps, which no current mission directly covers.

lessons.plain: When a team finishes building something, the first question is whether it matches what was agreed. A gap analysis compares three things: what was promised in the scope, what the requirements said the solution must do, and what was actually built. Any difference is a gap, sometimes called a delta. Some things were never built, some were built that nobody asked for, and some were built differently from how they were described. The business analyst's job is to find those differences, explain what each one means for the people who will use the solution, and make sure the right person decides what happens next.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team agreed to deliver a monthly statement export in PDF and an email reminder. At launch, only a CSV export exists, there is no reminder, and a dark-mode toggle has been added. Without any further reading, list the differences you would report, and say which one matters most to customers and why.
lessons.teach:
Scope is the set of work the solution is meant to include and exclude. A requirement is a specific statement of what the solution must do or hold, each given an ID so it can be tracked. The as-built state is what was actually delivered, which you can observe directly. A gap, also called a delta, is any mismatch between these three layers. There are three common kinds: a missing gap, where a requirement or in-scope item was never built; an extra gap, where something was built that no requirement or scope item asked for; and a divergent gap, where something exists but behaves differently from how it was specified.

Why it works: you check in both directions. Walking each requirement forward to its built evidence catches missing and divergent items. Walking each built feature backward to a requirement catches extras. A traceability matrix, a table linking requirement IDs to built items and test evidence, makes both walks visible and repeatable.

Worked example: Requirement R-12 says customers can download a monthly statement as a PDF. Step 1: find the built evidence for R-12; you find only a CSV download. Step 2: classify R-12 as divergent, since the format differs. Step 3: look for R-14, which asks for an email reminder on the first of each month; there is no built evidence, so it is missing. Step 4: find a dark-mode toggle that no requirement mentions; it is extra. Step 5: for each gap, record the impact, such as customers being unable to share statements in the format their bank accepts, and list the options: fix, defer, or accept through a change request.

Common mistake: reporting a list of differences with no impact statement and no decision owner. A bare list tells a sponsor nothing about whether to proceed.

Consequence: an unreported missing item often surfaces after deployment as a support ticket, when fixing it costs the most.

A gap analysis is complete only when every gap has a classification, a stated business impact, and a named person who decides what happens to it.

questions.prompt: A regional library's online reservation portal was delivered against a requirements list. R-07 says a reserved book is held for 48 hours before it returns to the shelf, and R-09 says members get a text message when a reserved book is ready. Built evidence shows the hold lasts 72 hours. No text message feature exists. A favourites shelf exists that no requirement mentions. Step 1: R-07 is matched to the 72-hour hold, so it is divergent because it exists but behaves differently from the specification. Step 2: R-09 has no built evidence, so it is missing. Step 3: the favourites shelf has no requirement behind it, so it is extra. Step 4 is missing from this worked example: what must be recorded and assigned for the R-07 divergence?
choices: Record that members who planned 48-hour pickups may lose items sooner, and name the branch manager to decide fix, defer, or accept.
Give R-07 a new ID so the mismatch is no longer linked to the original requirement in the traceability matrix, which keeps the matrix tidy for the sponsor review.
Delete the favourites shelf at once, because any built feature that no requirement mentions is a defect and must be removed before the library reopens.
Mark R-07 as closed, since a 72-hour hold still lets members collect their items in practice and the difference is small enough to ignore without anyone reviewing it.
questions.why: Every gap needs a stated business impact and a named decision owner, and option C records the impact on members and assigns the fix, defer, or accept decision.

questions.prompt: A food bank's volunteer sign-up app stores a scanned photo ID for each volunteer. No requirement or scope item asks for ID storage. Which gap type does this describe?
choices: Missing gap, because a requirement for ID storage was never built into the app.
Extra gap, because something was built that no requirement or scope item asked for.
Divergent gap, because the ID feature exists but behaves differently from its specification.
Not a gap, because storing extra data does no harm to the sign-up process.
questions.why: An extra gap is something built with no requirement or scope item behind it, which matches a stored photo ID that nothing asked for.

questions.prompt: A warehouse inventory system has requirement R-21, which says stock levels update within 5 seconds of a barcode scan. The as-built system updates stock in one end-of-shift batch, roughly 8 hours later. How should this mismatch be classified?
choices: Extra, because the end-of-shift batch job is a feature nobody asked for.
Divergent, because the update exists but its timing differs from the specified 5 seconds.
Missing, because the real-time update was never built into the system.
Not a gap, because the batch job runs every night without errors in testing.
questions.why: A divergent gap is something that exists but behaves differently from how it was specified, and the batch update exists but takes hours instead of seconds.

questions.prompt: A clinic's appointment tool team hands over a list of 14 mismatches between requirements and the built system. Each mismatch has a gap type assigned, but none has a stated business impact or a named decision owner. Is the gap analysis complete?
choices: No, because each gap still needs a stated business impact and a named person who decides what happens to it.
Yes, because gap types are the only required output and impact is a separate project activity.
No, because a traceability matrix must be rebuilt from scratch before any gap can be classified.
Yes, because all 14 differences were found and classified, which is enough for the sponsor to decide.
questions.why: A gap analysis is complete only when every gap has a classification, a stated business impact, and a named decision owner, and this list lacks the last two.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a delivery teammate how you would analyze and communicate the gaps between scope, requirements and what was built. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would walk the requirements forward to their built evidence and walk the built features backward to requirements, using a traceability matrix so nothing is skipped. Each mismatch gets classified as missing, extra, or divergent. For each one I state the business impact in plain terms, not just the technical difference, and propose options: fix before launch, defer, or accept through a change request. I send the sponsor a short gap register with a named decision owner for each item. The limit is that the analysis is only as good as the requirements. If a need was never written down, the traceability will not catch the missing behavior, so I also ask stakeholders what they expected to see but did not find documented.
rubricPoints: Defines scope, requirements and as-built state, and what a gap is
Checks in both directions: requirements to build, and build back to requirements
Classifies each gap as missing, extra or divergent
States business impact and options for each gap, with a named decision owner
Names a limit, such as gaps that come from unwritten needs

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine walks a learner through a gap register, so explaining the analysis and its impact back in their own words is the core skill.

lessons.plain: Sign-off is the moment the people who asked for a change formally say yes: this built thing does what we agreed, and it may go live. A business analyst does not decide that alone. Stakeholders are the people affected by the change, such as the users, the owner of the budget, and the team that will support it. Before asking for a yes, the analyst makes sure there is written evidence that the solution meets the agreed requirements, and that any gaps are visible to the people saying yes. The point is that going live is a decision someone accountable owns, not something that happens because the build finished.
lessons.guessPrompt: A developer says the new feature passed all its checks and is ready to ship. Who should decide whether it goes live, and what should that person need to see first?
lessons.teach:
Sign-off is a recorded approval from the named stakeholders who own the requirements, given after evidence shows the developed solution meets them. A stakeholder is anyone with a stake in the outcome, and the accountable one is the person with authority to accept the solution for use. Deployment means moving the solution into the live environment where real users depend on it. Sign-off is the gate between those two.

Why it works: a build being finished is not the same as a build being acceptable. Acceptance criteria are the measurable conditions agreed earlier that define done, for example an order must confirm within two seconds for 95 percent of requests. Sign-off checks the built solution against those conditions, using test results, demonstrations and a list of known gaps, and the stakeholder records a decision.

Worked example: a dispatch team asked for a route-change feature. First, the analyst lists the agreed acceptance criteria. Second, the testers report that 48 of 50 criteria pass. Third, the analyst records the two failing items: one cosmetic, and one that drops route changes made during a network outage. Fourth, the analyst presents this evidence to the dispatch manager and the operations owner. They choose a conditional sign-off: deploy once the outage defect is fixed and retested. The decision, its conditions, and the names of the approvers are written down.

Common mistake: treating a developer's 'it works' message, or a successful demo, as sign-off. A demo shows the happy path; sign-off needs evidence against the criteria and a named approver.

Consequence: without a recorded sign-off, nobody owns the risk after go-live. When the outage defect appears in production, no one can say who accepted it or on what evidence.

questions.prompt: A hospital billing team built an invoice-matching feature. Step 1: they listed 60 agreed acceptance criteria, which are the measurable conditions that define done. Step 2: testers reported that 57 of 60 pass. Step 3: the analyst recorded the three failures, including one that sends duplicate invoices to the payment queue when two users approve at the same time. Step 4 is missing from this account. What should happen next, before deployment?
choices: Present the three-gap evidence to the accountable approver and record their decision, any conditions, and the names of the approvers.
Run the matching feature live for one ward as a pilot to see whether duplicate invoices appear in practice.
Ask the lead developer to confirm in writing that the duplicate-invoice fix is done, then schedule deployment.
Rerun the demonstration for the finance director, because a clean demo is strong evidence that the feature is ready.
questions.why: Sign-off requires presenting the evidence against the criteria to the accountable approver, who records the decision, its conditions and the approvers' names, so the step that follows the gap list is that recorded approval.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes sign-off in this course?
choices: A successful demonstration of the main workflow shown to the project sponsor.
A recorded decision by the accountable approver, based on evidence against the agreed acceptance criteria.
The testers' written report that the solution has been run in the live environment.
The developer's confirmation that the build is complete and free of obvious errors.
questions.why: Sign-off is a recorded approval from the stakeholders who own the requirements, given after evidence shows the built solution meets the agreed criteria, and it is held by the accountable approver.

questions.prompt: A team's chatbot passes a live demo of ten typical customer questions. Which is the strongest reason this does not yet amount to sign-off?
choices: The testers ran the demo rather than the developers, so the result is not valid for approval purposes.
Deployment can begin as soon as the demo succeeds, because the sponsor watched it and was satisfied with the result.
A demo shows only the happy path, with no evidence against agreed criteria and no named approver recorded.
Sign-off requires the demo to be repeated until every possible customer question gets a perfect answer.
questions.why: A demo shows the happy path only; sign-off needs evidence measured against the agreed criteria and a named approver's recorded decision, and neither is present here.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder says the team can deploy now because 19 of 20 acceptance criteria pass and the one failure is cosmetic. What is the right response?
choices: Present the 19 of 20 result and the cosmetic gap to the accountable approver for a recorded decision.
Hold deployment until all 20 criteria pass, since partial results never count toward any decision.
Ask the developer to confirm the cosmetic issue is harmless, then deploy without further review.
Deploy immediately, since a cosmetic failure carries no business risk at all.
questions.why: The team should present the evidence and the known gap to the accountable approver, who records the decision, rather than deciding alone or treating a single failure as automatically acceptable or blocking.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a stakeholder sign-off should contain before a solution goes to deployment, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on it, such as what it cannot guarantee after go-live.
lessons.modelAnswer: Before deployment, sign-off should be a recorded decision by the stakeholders who own the requirements. It should point to evidence: test results measured against the agreed acceptance criteria, a list of known gaps or defects with their severity, and a statement of the scope that was actually built. The decision is one of accept, accept with conditions, or reject, and it names the approver and the date. The main limit is that sign-off reflects what was known and tested at that moment. It cannot guarantee the solution will behave correctly under real load or with data nobody tested, and approvers may accept a risk they did not fully understand. So the analyst should keep the accepted gaps visible after go-live and later check the outcome against the business case.
rubricPoints: Sign-off is a recorded decision by accountable stakeholders, not a team's own claim that the work is finished.
The sign-off should rest on test evidence measured against agreed acceptance criteria.
Known gaps and defects, with severity, must be disclosed so approvers accept risk knowingly.
Sign-off reflects what was tested at that time and cannot guarantee behaviour under untested conditions.

suggested.rationale: Sign-off is a judgement and communication skill, best checked by the learner explaining the decision and its limits in their own words.

lessons.plain: Once a solution is live, the question changes from 'does it work?' to 'did it deliver the reason we funded it?' A business case is the written argument for spending money or effort: the problem, the options, the expected gains and the cost. A value proposition is the short statement of what the change gives the people who use or pay for it. Evaluating the deployed solution means comparing what actually happened after go-live with those original promises, using measures agreed up front. A system can run perfectly and still fail this test if the people it was meant to help never use it, or the expected savings never appear. Your job is to show the evidence, not just the feeling that it went well.
lessons.guessPrompt: A new online booking form is live and its logs show no errors. The business case promised a fifth fewer phone calls to the call centre within six months. What single piece of evidence would tell you more about whether the project succeeded than the error logs?
lessons.teach:
Evaluating a deployed solution against the business case means checking whether the benefits the case promised have actually appeared in the live environment, not only whether the solution meets its requirements. Three terms matter here. The business case is the documented reason for the investment: the problem, the options considered, the expected benefits, the costs and the timeline. The value proposition is the short statement of what the change should give its users or sponsors. A success measure is a specific, observable number tied to one benefit, such as calls per month or minutes to complete an order, with a baseline recorded before go-live so you have something to compare against.

Why this works: requirements tell you the solution does what was specified, but a solution can match every requirement and still fail to move the number that justified it. Comparing post-deployment measures against the baseline and the target separates delivered value from delivered features.

Worked example: a team built a self-service returns portal aiming to cut returns-related calls by 20 percent within six months. Step 1: take the baseline, which was 1,000 calls a month. Step 2: after three months live, the count is 960, a 4 percent drop. Step 3: review call reasons and find that customers with gift orders still cannot look up their order, so they still phone. Step 4: report the gap between target and actual, with its cause, to the sponsor before sign-off.

Common mistake: declaring success because the portal has no defects and launched on schedule. Those are delivery facts, not benefit facts.

Consequence: if the gap is not reported, the organisation keeps paying for a solution that does not fix the problem, and the next funding decision rests on a false picture.

questions.prompt: A credit union launched an online loan pre-approval form to cut the average time from application to decision from 4.5 days to a target of 2.0 days. Step 1: the 4.5-day baseline was recorded before go-live. Step 2: after 90 days live, the average is 3.5 days. Step 3 is missing and is the step that turns these figures into a benefit finding. Which choice completes step 3?
choices: Report that the form passed every acceptance test and launched on schedule, which proves the benefit is delivered.
Confirm that all loan officers attended training before the sponsor signs off on the project plan.
Reset the baseline to the 3.5-day figure so that the new average looks like the starting point for the next target.
Calculate the gap: 1.0 day achieved against a 2.5-day target, which is 40 percent of the promise, then report it with its cause.
questions.why: The benefit is judged by comparing the measured change against the baseline and the target, so the achieved share of the promised improvement must be calculated and reported with its cause.

questions.prompt: Which statement best defines a success measure as used when evaluating a deployed solution against its business case?
choices: The sponsor's signed approval of the business case document, which lists the problem and the options considered.
A complete list of every requirement the solution meets, checked against the original specification document.
A tally of defects closed during the final test cycle before the chosen launch date was set.
A specific, observable number tied to one benefit, with a baseline recorded before go-live so it can be compared later.
questions.why: A success measure is defined as a specific observable number linked to one benefit, with a pre-go-live baseline for comparison.

questions.prompt: A hospital added automated appointment reminder texts. The goal was to cut the no-show rate from 18 percent to 12 percent. Four months after launch, the no-show rate is 17 percent, and every reminder text was delivered without error. What is the correct evaluation conclusion?
choices: Sign-off should wait until the 12 percent target is reached, whatever the cause of the remaining gap turns out to be.
Only about one of the six points of promised reduction has appeared, so the gap and its cause should be reported to the sponsor before sign-off.
The baseline should be thrown away because four months is too short a period to judge any change at all.
The solution delivered its value because every reminder text was delivered without error and no defects were logged.
questions.why: Comparing the measured rate with the baseline and target shows that only a small part of the promised benefit has appeared, and the gap must be reported with its cause rather than replaced by delivery facts.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm built a route-planning app for drivers, expecting to cut fuel cost per delivery by 8 percent. The team reports that all user stories were accepted, no defects are open, and the app went live two weeks early. Fuel cost per delivery has not changed, and no figure was recorded before go-live. What is the main failure in how this solution is being evaluated?
choices: Without a baseline recorded before go-live, the fuel figures cannot be compared, so delivery facts are being mistaken for evidence of value.
The app was delivered too early, so drivers had no time to adopt it before the fuel figures were taken.
The user stories were incomplete, which is the most likely reason the fuel target was missed.
The eight percent target was too ambitious, so the sponsor should lower it to whatever the current figure shows.
questions.why: The evaluation cannot show whether the promised benefit appeared because no pre-go-live baseline exists, and the team is relying on delivery facts instead of benefit facts.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has just finished testing how evaluating a deployed solution against the business case differs from confirming it meets requirements, and name one limit of this kind of evaluation, such as timing or attributing cause.
lessons.modelAnswer: Testing confirms the solution does what the requirements said, so it answers whether we built it right. Evaluating against the business case asks whether the benefits we promised show up in live use, which is whether we built the right thing for the reason we funded it. The two can disagree: a portal can pass every test and still leave customers calling because a key case was missed. To evaluate, we take the success measures from the business case, compare the pre-go-live baseline with post-go-live figures over an agreed period, and explain any gap with evidence. The main limit is timing and attribution. Benefits can take months to appear, so an early reading may understate them, and other changes, like a price cut, can move the same number, so we cannot always credit the solution alone. We should state those limits in the report rather than present one figure as proof.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes meeting requirements from delivering the benefits promised in the business case.
Compares post-deployment measures against a pre-go-live baseline and the agreed target.
Explains any gap with evidence about its cause, not just the size of the number.
Names a limit such as benefit timing lag or attributing change to other factors.

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through an exam-style post-go-live situation with conflicting signals builds the judgement this objective needs more than any listed mission does.

scenarios.title: Harbourline Freight dispatch scheduling
scenarios.scenario: Harbourline Freight is a fictional regional trucking company with about 140 drivers and four depots. Dispatchers currently build each day's delivery routes in a spreadsheet and confirm changes by phone. When a truck breaks down or a customer moves a delivery window, the re-plan often takes two hours, and about one delivery in twelve is late. The operations director has proposed a new route scheduling tool and asked you, as the project's business analyst, to assess the need before any tool is chosen. Business analysis here means studying a problem and working out what change would fix it. A problem statement is a short, plain description of the gap between how things are and how they should be. A solution scope statement is a written boundary that says what the initiative will deliver and what it will not. A value proposition is the specific benefit the initiative offers, stated so it can be checked, and for whom. A stakeholder is any person or group who affects, or is affected by, the initiative. Elicitation means the structured ways you draw out information from people and documents, such as interviews, workshops, and reviewing records. The director's written request reads: 'Late deliveries are costing us money. Buy a scheduling tool and fix it.' Work through the following. 1. Rewrite the director's request as a problem statement and draft a solution scope statement that separates what the new tool should do from what is out of scope, such as driver pay rules or fleet purchasing. 2. Using the delivery records, the dispatcher notes, and the customer complaint log you have been given, state the value proposition as a measurable benefit with a baseline figure you could verify later. 3. The request names only dispatchers and the director. List the other stakeholder groups who should be identified and say briefly why each one matters. 4. Describe how you would elicit each group's values, meaning what they care about most, so the team has a baseline for ranking requirements later.
subParts: Value proposition with a measurable baseline
Elicitation of stakeholder values as a prioritization baseline
modelAnswer: A strong answer restates the request as a gap, for example: Roughly one in twelve deliveries is late, and each re-plan after a disruption takes about two hours of dispatcher time, because route changes are made by phone and tracked in spreadsheets. The solution scope statement should say the initiative will deliver a system for building and changing daily routes after disruptions, covering the four depots and the current driver roster. It should explicitly exclude driver pay rules, fleet purchasing, and customer billing, and name any integration with the existing delivery-tracking system as in scope or out of scope. A weak answer just repeats 'buy a tool' or leaves the boundary vague, which lets later requests pile on unrelated work.

A strong answer states the value as a measurable change from a verified baseline, for example: reduce late deliveries from about 8 percent (the figure in the last six months of records) to under 4 percent within six months of go-live, and cut the average disruption re-plan time from about two hours to under thirty minutes. It names who gets the benefit, such as dispatchers, depot managers, and customers, and says how each figure will be checked. A common mistake is to state a value like 'better efficiency' that nobody can measure or test. Without a baseline, the team cannot tell later whether the initiative delivered anything.

A strong answer names groups beyond the director and dispatchers, such as drivers (who receive and act on the routes), depot managers (who own delivery performance at their site), customer service staff (who field complaints and rebook deliveries), the IT team that runs the current tracking system and will support any new tool, the finance team that tracks cost of late deliveries and overtime, and customers or key account managers who feel the effect of late deliveries. For each group, the answer gives a reason, such as drivers needing routes that match actual working hours, or IT needing to know about data and integration impact. A common mistake is to list only the people who raised the request, which leaves out the people who will use or be affected by the result.

A strong answer chooses elicitation methods that fit each group, for example structured interviews with dispatchers and depot managers to learn what slows re-planning, a short workshop with drivers to learn what makes a route unworkable, a review of complaint logs and cost records for customer and finance values, and a working session with IT on constraints. Each method should produce a ranked list of what each group values, such as speed of re-planning, accuracy of arrival times, or fewer phone calls. The answer should say that these ranked values become the baseline used to prioritize requirements, and that conflicting values, such as dispatchers wanting full control while drivers want fixed routes, will be recorded and resolved with the sponsor rather than silently dropped. A common mistake is to treat the director's view as the only value set, which skews later priorities toward one group.

scenarios.title: Returns Portal Requirements Kickoff at Brightwater Parcel Co.
scenarios.scenario: Brightwater Parcel Co. is a fictional mid-sized parcel delivery firm. Its customer returns are handled through a web form and a spreadsheet that the warehouse team and the customer service team both edit. The company has approved a project to replace this with a Returns Portal, and the business analyst, Priya, is about to start requirements work. The business case says the goal is to cut the average time to process a return from 9 days to under 3 days and to reduce duplicate refund payments. Priya must set up the planning artifacts before elicitation begins. A traceability matrix is a table that links each requirement to its source and to the design and test items that implement it, so that you can see at a glance what depends on what. A baseline is a version of a document that has been reviewed and approved and is used as the reference point for all later changes. Acceptance criteria are the specific, testable conditions a solution must meet before the business accepts it. Sub-tasks: 1. Describe the traceability strategy Priya should define, naming the links to trace and the tool or technique she would use to keep them current. 2. Select a change-control method for requirements and explain how a proposed change moves from request to incorporation into the change management plan. 3. Explain how Priya should apply document control to the requirements package, including versioning and when a baseline is set. 4. Describe how Priya should define business metrics and acceptance criteria with the stakeholders, giving one example of each that could be checked after go-live.
subParts: Traceability strategy: links to trace and the tool or technique to keep them current
Change-control method and how a request flows into the change management plan
Document control: versioning and when a baseline is set
Business metrics and acceptance criteria defined with stakeholders, with one checkable example each
modelAnswer: Priya should trace each business requirement (for example, refund within 3 days) to the stakeholder request that raised it, then to the solution requirements that implement it, then to the test cases that verify it. She should record these links in a traceability matrix kept in the requirements management tool so that each row shows source, requirement, design element and test case. She should assign an owner to update the matrix whenever a requirement is added or changed, and review it at each stage gate. A common mistake is building the matrix once at the end of analysis and never updating it; then impact analysis for later changes is wrong because nobody can see the dependencies.

The standard method is a change request form. Any stakeholder submits a change request describing the proposed change, the reason, and the requirements it touches. Priya then performs an impact assessment, estimating effects on cost, schedule, other requirements and the business case. The change control board, made up of the sponsor, a process owner and a technical lead, approves, rejects or defers the change. Approved changes are logged, the traceability matrix is updated, and the change is written into the change management plan so that every later change follows the same route. Rejected changes are also logged with the reason, so the same request is not reopened without new information.

Priya should store the requirements package in a controlled repository where each document carries a version number and an approval status such as draft, in review or approved. Only one person checks out a document at a time, so two people do not overwrite each other. A baseline is set once the stakeholders have reviewed and signed off the requirements for the current scope. After that point, any change to a baseline must go through change control and produces a new version number, so the team can always show what was agreed on a given date. A mistake to avoid is editing the approved file directly; the team then loses the record of what was agreed.

Priya should run a workshop with the sponsor, the warehouse lead and the customer service lead to agree on business metrics and acceptance criteria. A business metric is a measurable result the business cares about. Example metric: average days from return request to refund, measured monthly from portal timestamps, with a target of under 3 days. An acceptance criterion is a testable condition. Example: when a return is submitted with a valid tracking number, the system must create a single refund instruction, and a duplicate submission for the same tracking number must be blocked, verified by a test with 50 sample returns. Each criterion should be written so that a tester could pass or fail it without asking the author what it meant.

scenarios.title: Marlow Parcels returns portal: turning vague requests into a checkable baseline
scenarios.scenario: Marlow Parcels is a fictional mid-size online retailer. Its returns team wants a self-service returns portal so customers can start a return without calling support. Raw input has come from interviews and a shared notes document. Three items stand out. (a) The warehouse lead says refunds should be quick. (b) The finance controller says each refund must post to the general ledger (the company's master record of money in and out) within one business day after the warehouse confirms the returned item was received. (c) The customer-service manager wants a live chat button inside the portal. The sponsor has said this is nice to have but has not decided. A requirement is a statement of something the solution must do or be. Decomposition means breaking a broad requirement into smaller parts that can each be built and tested. A dependency is a link where one item cannot be finished or tested until another item is done. An interface is a point where two systems or groups exchange information, such as the warehouse scanner feed into the portal. A requirements baseline is the agreed set of requirements the project will build against. Work through the following. 1. Decompose item (a) into testable requirements, and name the dependencies it has on item (b) and on the warehouse scanner interface. 2. Recommend accept, defer, or reject for item (c) using simple weighted scoring: give it a 1 to 5 score for business value and a 1 to 5 score for effort, explain your reasoning, and say whether it belongs in the baseline now. 3. Write one measurable acceptance criterion for refund posting that a tester could check using a sample of returns.
subParts: Decompose item (a) into testable requirements and name its dependencies on item (b) and the warehouse scanner interface.
Recommend accept, defer, or reject for the live chat item using weighted scoring, and state whether it enters the baseline.
Write one measurable acceptance criterion for refund posting that a tester can check with a sample of returns.
modelAnswer: Vague wording like quick refunds cannot be built or tested, so it must be broken into parts that each have a clear condition. A sound decomposition splits item (a) into at least three requirements: (1) the portal shows the customer a refund status that updates when the warehouse confirms receipt; (2) the system records the time of warehouse confirmation as a timestamp in the returns record; (3) the refund is issued to the original payment method once confirmation is recorded. Each one names a trigger and an observable result. The dependency on item (b) is that requirement (3) cannot be fully tested until the ledger posting rule exists, because a refund that is issued but not posted does not meet the finance control. The dependency on the scanner interface is that requirement (2) relies on the scanner feed sending a receipt event with a usable timestamp; if the feed sends only a batch file at end of day, the timestamp will be wrong and the one-day rule will be hard to meet. Common mistake: writing the decomposition as a list of features instead of conditions, so testers cannot tell when the requirement is met. Consequence: if the scanner dependency is missed, the team may build a real-time refund flow that the warehouse system cannot feed, and the schedule slips when the gap is found during testing.

Weighted scoring means giving each option a score on several criteria, multiplying each by a weight that shows its importance, and adding the results so options can be compared on one scale. Here the scores are simple: business value 2 out of 5 (support staff would like it, but the notes show no measured drop in calls or returns caused by a lack of chat) and effort 4 out of 5 (chat needs a third-party provider, staffing rules, and security review, which is high effort for the one release). A simple reading is that value is low and effort is high, so the item should be deferred rather than accepted. Reject would be wrong, because the sponsor has not ruled it out and the need is real. Accepting it into the baseline now would add scope that competes with the refund rules, which are needed for the finance control. The recommendation is to defer: record the item with its origin (the customer-service manager, in the interview notes), its rationale, and a review date after the first release, and keep it out of the current requirements baseline. Common mistake: scoring only value and ignoring effort, which makes every stakeholder request look worth building. Consequence: an unscored chat feature in the baseline would compete for the same build and test time as the refund posting rule, which may put the one-day finance rule at risk.

A measurable acceptance criterion states a condition, a sample, and a pass threshold so that a tester can give a clear yes or no. For refund posting, a usable version is: for a test sample of 50 returns received by the warehouse on a set of business days, at least 95 percent of refunds must show a ledger posting entry dated within one business day after the warehouse receipt timestamp, and no refund may post before the receipt timestamp exists. The sample size, the threshold, and the time reference are all stated, so a tester can compute the result from the records. Common mistake: writing a criterion such as refunds must post quickly, which gives the tester no way to say pass or fail. Consequence: without a threshold, the team can argue after testing that the result was good enough, and the finance controller may later find refunds posted late that the test seemed to accept.

scenarios.title: Freight Invoice Reconciliation Change at Brightwell Freight Systems
scenarios.scenario:
Brightwell Freight Systems is a fictional mid-sized trucking company that is replacing its old spreadsheet-based invoice checking with a new billing module. You are the business analyst on the project, and the project manager, Priya, has asked you to keep the requirements under control. A requirement is a stated need the solution must meet. A traceability tool is a register, such as a matrix or a tool database, that links each requirement to the business objective it supports, the design model that describes it, the test cases that prove it, and its current status. A lifecycle state is one stage a requirement passes through, such as proposed, approved, built, verified, or accepted. The requirements baseline is the agreed, versioned set of approved requirements that the project measures change against. The change-control plan is the agreed process for how a proposed change is logged, assessed, and approved, usually by a change-control board, which is the group of stakeholders who decide whether changes go ahead.

Requirement REQ-114 says the billing module must reject any freight invoice where the billed weight is above the contracted weight tier of 500 kg without an approved surcharge code. It traces to business objective BO-03, which is to cut billing disputes by a fixed amount. It is described in design model DM-22 and tested by test cases TC-410 and TC-411. Last week, the build team finished REQ-114 and TC-410 passed in the test environment. TC-411 has not been run yet because its test data is still being prepared. Baseline version 2.3 is current.
