This morning a customer manager asked for the weight tier to be raised from 500 kg to 750 kg. Change request CR-07 has been logged, and the change-control board meets on Thursday. Related requirement REQ-119 controls the monthly rate report, which reads the same weight tier value.

Please complete the following:

1. Describe exactly how you would record REQ-114's current status and evidence in the traceability tool, naming the lifecycle state you would set and the links you would add or check.

2. Assess the impact of CR-07 on the requirements baseline. Identify which artifacts and requirements are affected, what dependencies exist, what risk the change creates, and what must happen before any rework begins under the change-control plan.

3. Write a short status update to Priya and the stakeholders covering REQ-114's progress, the open change, the risk you identified, and any conflict or issue they need to decide on.
subParts: Record REQ-114 status and evidence in the traceability tool
Assess the impact of CR-07 on the baseline
Communicate status, risks, and decisions needed
modelAnswer: Set REQ-114 to the verified state, not accepted, because TC-410 has passed but TC-411 is still pending and stakeholder acceptance has not been given. Add or confirm the links from REQ-114 up to BO-03 and down to DM-22, TC-410, and TC-411, and attach the TC-410 pass result as evidence with the date, tester, and build identifier. Mark TC-411 as not yet executed so the gap is visible, and note the reason (test data in preparation). Record the status change with the date, the person making it, and the reason, so the history shows why the state moved. Leave the accepted state empty until the business sponsor signs off.

CR-07 changes a value that appears in REQ-114 (the 500 kg threshold) and REQ-119 (the monthly rate report), so both are affected. Artifacts affected include DM-22, TC-410, TC-411, and the report specification for REQ-119. Dependencies: REQ-119 reads the same tier value, so changing REQ-114 without REQ-119 would produce inconsistent results between billing and reporting. The main risk is that the new 750 kg tier silently breaks the existing rejection logic or the report, and that BO-03 (dispute reduction) may be weakened if invoices between 500 and 750 kg are no longer checked. Under the change-control plan, the change must be logged against baseline 2.3 and assessed by the change-control board on Thursday before any rework on REQ-114 or REQ-119 starts. The baseline should not be altered until the board approves CR-07, and the approved version becomes the new baseline.

Keep the update short and factual. State that REQ-114 is built and passed its first test (TC-410) and is waiting on TC-411 before it can be accepted. Report CR-07 as logged, with the impact on REQ-114, REQ-119, and the test cases, and state that no rework will start until the change-control board decides on Thursday. Name the risk clearly: a changed weight tier could affect the monthly report and the dispute-reduction goal. Ask for the decisions needed: whether the customer's 750 kg tier is approved, whether the monthly report should change at the same time, and whether TC-411 test data can be prioritized so the requirement can be accepted. Give Priya the issue and the conflict between the customer's request and the current objective, so she can take it to the board, and avoid mixing these items into a general 'all good' summary.

scenarios.title: Returns Self-Service Portal at Brightwater Parcels
scenarios.scenario:
Brightwater Parcels Ltd is a fictional regional parcel-delivery company. Its project team has built a customer self-service returns portal, where customers print return labels and track refunds without phoning the service desk. The business analyst (BA) on the project, Priya, is preparing the evaluation work for the steering group. Some terms first: acceptance criteria are the measurable conditions a solution must meet to be accepted, a traceability matrix is a table that links each requirement to its design, test cases and results, user acceptance testing (UAT) is testing carried out by business users on the real workflow before release, a gap is any difference between what was required or approved and what was actually delivered, and a business case is the document justifying the investment, stating the expected benefits and how they will be measured. The UAT log shows 118 test cases run, 109 passed, 6 failed and 3 were not run because the test environment lacked sample refund data. Five of the nine acceptance criteria point to test cases that passed. Criterion AC-4 requires a refund status to appear within 2 minutes of the refund being approved in the finance system. The only evidence for AC-4 is a demo recording from a sandbox where the finance feed was simulated. The approved scope also included a 'lost parcel claim' form, which is absent from the build, and the change log shows no approved change removing it. The steering group wants a go or no-go decision next week. Complete the following:

1. Review the UAT results and evidence against the acceptance criteria. State which criteria are proven, which are not, and what the six failures and three unrun cases mean for the release decision.

2. Identify the gaps between the approved scope, the requirements and what was built. Classify each gap and explain how you would communicate them to the sponsor so the decision is informed.

3. Set out the conditions Priya should attach to stakeholder sign-off before the solution proceeds to deployment, and say who must give that sign-off.

4. Three months after release, the business case projected a 25 percent drop in calls to the service desk for returns within six months. Explain how you would evaluate the deployed solution against that business case and the value proposition, and what you would report if the call volume fell by only 8 percent.
subParts: Review UAT results and evidence against acceptance criteria
Analyse and communicate scope, requirement and build gaps
Set sign-off conditions and identify who signs off
Evaluate the deployed solution against the business case
modelAnswer: Proven criteria are those where a passing test case directly exercises the criterion in a realistic environment. Five of nine criteria are proven by passing UAT cases. AC-4 is not proven, because the only evidence is a demo in a sandbox with a simulated finance feed, which does not show the real two-minute timing. Two further criteria should be checked against the traceability matrix to confirm which failed or unrun cases map to them. The six failures must each be classified as blocking or non-blocking, and any failure touching a criterion must be treated as blocking until fixed and retested. The three unrun cases are not evidence of anything, so they count as untested. The release decision should therefore be conditional, not a clean go: the team can only claim acceptance for the proven criteria and must show retest results for AC-4 and the failures. A common mistake is to report '109 of 118 passed, 92 percent success' as if that proves readiness; the pass rate hides which requirements are actually untested.

Gaps are differences between what was approved or required and what was delivered. The missing lost parcel claim form is a scope gap, because it was in approved scope and no approved change removed it. AC-4 is a verification gap, because the requirement exists but was not shown to work in the real environment. The unrun test cases are a coverage gap. Each gap should be recorded with its source document, its impact on customers and operations, and a recommended option: deliver now, defer with a documented change request, or accept the risk with a named owner. Communicate them to the sponsor in one short table or summary, stating what the decision options are and what each costs in time or risk. Do not soften the missing form by calling it a minor enhancement, because the change log contradicts that. The consequence of hiding a scope gap is that the business case benefits assume a claim process that customers cannot use.

Sign-off conditions should be specific and testable: AC-4 retested against the live finance feed with timing recorded; all blocking failures fixed and retested with evidence; the three unrun cases either executed or formally accepted as a risk by the owner; the missing lost parcel claim form either built, or removed through an approved change with the sponsor's agreement; and the traceability matrix updated so each criterion points to real passing evidence. Sign-off should come from the business sponsor who owns the benefits, the operations lead for the service desk who will run the solution, and the finance representative for the refund integration. The BA records the sign-off with date, version and the conditions met. A common mistake is letting the project manager alone give approval, because the people who must live with the outcome were not asked. If sign-off is given without these conditions, the portal goes live with an untested refund path, and customers may be told refunds arrive in two minutes when they do not.

Evaluating the deployed solution means comparing measured results with the business case, not with the project's own sense of success. Priya should first confirm the baseline: the service desk call volume for returns before release, measured over a comparable period. She then measures the same metric after release, adjusting for seasonality such as peak parcel periods. The business case expected a 25 percent reduction within six months, so at three months she should look at the trend and at the portion of the target that has been reached, while being clear that the final verdict needs the full period. An 8 percent drop is a partial result. The report should state the measured change, the expected change, the time elapsed, and whether the shortfall comes from low adoption, from customers using the portal but still calling, or from a missing feature such as the claim form. It should also recommend actions: promote the portal in the returns confirmation message, review the call reasons, and reassess the target with the sponsor. The value proposition should be restated in measurable terms, and the report should not claim success on the basis that the portal works technically. Overclaiming the result is the most common mistake, and it damages trust in future business cases.
